nodes.title: Knowing Our Numbers: Large Numbers and Estimation
nodes.description: You will read, write, compare and order large numbers in both the Indian (lakh, crore) and international (million, billion) systems, and use rounding to estimate sums, differences and products. Estimation is the everyday superpower of mathematics: it lets you sanity-check bills, budgets and news headlines in seconds.
learning_outcomes: Can read and write numbers up to crores using both Indian and international place-value systems, with correct comma placement
Can compare and order large numbers by aligning place values, not just by looking at leading digits
Can round a number to the nearest ten, hundred, thousand or lakh
Can estimate the result of an addition, subtraction or multiplication and judge whether an exact answer is reasonable

misconceptions.description: Compares numbers by their leading digits instead of by number of digits and place value (e.g. thinks 98,765 > 1,00,065 because 9 > 1).
misconceptions.signal: Says the number starting with the bigger digit is bigger, even when the other number has more digits.
misconceptions.remedy: Have the student count digits first and stack numbers right-aligned in a place-value chart; compare column by column from the left only after digit counts match.

misconceptions.description: Confuses the Indian and international systems, e.g. believes 1 lakh = 1 million.
misconceptions.signal: Writes 10,00,000 when asked for one lakh, or reads 5,000,000 as 'five lakh'.
misconceptions.remedy: Build a two-row conversion strip (1 lakh = 100 thousand, 10 lakh = 1 million, 1 crore = 10 million) and practise re-punctuating the same digit string with both comma conventions.

misconceptions.description: When rounding, looks at the wrong digit (often the last digit) instead of the digit just below the rounding place.
misconceptions.signal: Rounds 8,468 to the nearest thousand as 9,000 'because it ends in 8'.
misconceptions.remedy: Teach an explicit two-step routine: underline the rounding place, circle the single digit to its right, and let only the circled digit decide up or down; verify on a number line showing which thousand is nearer.

misconceptions.description: Thinks estimation is random guessing rather than controlled rounding, so estimates wildly or refuses to estimate without computing exactly.
misconceptions.signal: Computes the exact answer first and then 'estimates' by copying it, or offers a guess unconnected to the numbers.
misconceptions.remedy: Give estimation-only tasks with a strict time budget where exact computation is impossible, then compare classmates' rounded estimates against the exact value to show the method's reliability.

real_world_hooks: Populations of Indian cities in a census table: which is bigger, 92,53,000 or 1,02,10,000?
IPL auction amounts: is 12 crore more or less than 120 million?
Estimating a monthly grocery bill before the shopkeeper totals it

questions.prompt: Which of these numbers is the greatest?

options.diagnosis: Chose the number with the most repeated large digits; not attending to the number of digits at all.

questions.explanation: Count digits first: 1,00,065 has six digits while 98,765 and 99,999 have five and 9,999 has four. A six-digit number is always greater than any five-digit number, so 1,00,065 (one lakh sixty-five) is the greatest, even though it starts with 1.

questions.prompt: Round 8,468 to the nearest thousand.

options.diagnosis: Rounded to the nearest five hundred instead of the nearest thousand.
Rounded to the nearest ten; misread which place value was asked for.

questions.explanation: The thousands digit is 8. The digit just to its right (hundreds) is 4, which is less than 5, so we round down: 8,468 → 8,000. The final 8 in the ones place plays no role in rounding to the nearest thousand.

questions.prompt: A school collected ₹5,290 in week 1 and ₹17,986 in week 2. Estimate the total collection by rounding each amount to the nearest thousand.

options.diagnosis: Rounded both numbers down (truncated) instead of rounding to the nearest thousand.
Rounded both numbers up regardless of the hundreds digit.

questions.explanation: 5,290 rounds to 5,000 (hundreds digit 2 < 5) and 17,986 rounds to 18,000 (hundreds digit 9 ≥ 5). Estimated total: 5,000 + 18,000 = ₹23,000. Note ₹23,276 is the exact sum — a correct calculation, but not an estimate, which is what was asked.

nodes.title: Whole Numbers and Their Properties
nodes.description: Whole numbers are the counting numbers together with zero. You will explore their behaviour on the number line and the properties of addition and multiplication — commutativity, associativity, distributivity and the special roles of 0 and 1 — and use these properties to compute cleverly instead of laboriously.
learning_outcomes: Can identify predecessors and successors and locate whole numbers on a number line
Can state which operations on whole numbers are commutative and associative, with counterexamples for subtraction and division
Can use distributivity and regrouping to simplify calculations such as 8 × 293 × 125 mentally
Can explain the roles of 0 and 1 as identities and why division by zero is undefined

misconceptions.description: Believes dividing by zero gives zero (or gives the number itself).
misconceptions.signal: Writes 7 ÷ 0 = 0 or 7 ÷ 0 = 7 without hesitation.
misconceptions.remedy: Recast division as 'how many groups?': 7 ÷ 0 asks how many groups of 0 make 7 — no number of empty groups ever reaches 7. Contrast with 0 ÷ 7 = 0, which does make sense.

misconceptions.description: Assumes subtraction and division are commutative like addition and multiplication.
misconceptions.signal: Claims 5 − 8 = 8 − 5 or rearranges a − b to b − a mid-calculation 'because order doesn't matter'.
misconceptions.remedy: Have the student test each property with small concrete numbers before using it, and keep a personal 'property table' showing which operations pass and fail the order-swap test.

misconceptions.description: Thinks 1 (not 0) is the smallest whole number, or that zero is 'nothing' and not a number.
misconceptions.signal: Starts the whole-number list at 1, or refuses to place 0 on the number line.
misconceptions.remedy: Distinguish natural numbers from whole numbers explicitly, and use contexts where 0 is a meaningful value (0 runs scored, 0°C, floor 0) rather than an absence.

misconceptions.description: Misapplies distributivity, e.g. 4 × (25 + 3) = 4 × 25 + 3, distributing over only the first term.
misconceptions.signal: Multiplies only one addend inside the bracket by the outside factor.
misconceptions.remedy: Draw the rectangle/area model: a 4-by-28 rectangle split into 4-by-25 and 4-by-3 parts makes visible that BOTH parts get multiplied by 4.

real_world_hooks: Mental math at a shop: 8 packets at ₹293 each, grouped as 8 × 125 tricks with round numbers
Cricket: a batter on 0 runs — zero as a real score, not 'nothing'
Splitting a UPI payment: why ₹0 sent leaves the balance unchanged (additive identity)
teaching.video_search: whole numbers properties commutative associative distributive class 6

questions.prompt: What is the smallest whole number?

options.diagnosis: Reaching ahead to integers; negative numbers are not whole numbers.

options.text: There is no smallest whole number
options.diagnosis: Confusing 'no largest' (true) with 'no smallest' (false) — the list stops going down at 0.

questions.explanation: Whole numbers are 0, 1, 2, 3, … The collection has no largest member, but it does have a smallest: 0. (The natural numbers 1, 2, 3, … are the whole numbers without zero — that is where the '1' answer comes from.)

questions.prompt: Using a clever regrouping, find 8 × 293 × 125.

options.diagnosis: Correct method (8 × 125 = 1000) but dropped a zero when multiplying by 1000.
Correct method but added an extra zero when multiplying by 1000.
Treated 8 × 125 as 100 instead of 1000, then computed 2344 × 100.

questions.explanation: Multiplication is commutative and associative, so regroup: 8 × 125 = 1000, and 1000 × 293 = 293,000. The whole point of the properties is to pair numbers that make powers of ten.

questions.prompt: Which statement is true for EVERY whole number a?

options.diagnosis: Confusing a ÷ a (which is 1, when a ≠ 0) with a − a = 0.

questions.explanation: Subtracting zero changes nothing, so a − 0 = a always holds. Division by zero is undefined (not zero). Subtraction is not commutative, so 0 − a is not a for a > 0 (it is not even a whole number). And a ÷ a = 1 for a ≠ 0, while it is a − a that equals 0.

nodes.title: Factors, Multiples, Divisibility, HCF and LCM
nodes.description: Numbers have hidden structure: factors, multiples, primes and composites. You will learn divisibility tests, prime factorisation, and how to find the HCF (highest common factor) and LCM (lowest common multiple) of numbers — tools you will use constantly with fractions, ratios and repeating events.
learning_outcomes: Can list factors and multiples of a number and classify numbers as prime or composite
Can apply divisibility tests for 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10 and 11
Can find HCF and LCM using prime factorisation and choose which one a word problem needs
Can verify and use the relation HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers

misconceptions.description: Believes 1 is a prime number (or that 2 is not prime because it is even).
misconceptions.signal: Includes 1 when listing primes, or excludes 2 saying 'even numbers can't be prime'.
misconceptions.remedy: Return to the definition — a prime has exactly two distinct factors. Count factors of 1 (just one factor) and of 2 (exactly two: 1 and 2) to settle both cases at once.

misconceptions.description: Swaps HCF and LCM: gives the LCM when the highest common factor is asked, and vice versa.
misconceptions.signal: Answers 36 for the HCF of 12 and 18, or 6 for their LCM.
misconceptions.remedy: Anchor the words: the HCF is a FACTOR so it fits inside both numbers (≤ both); the LCM is a MULTIPLE so both numbers fit inside it (≥ both). Have the student sanity-check every answer against this size rule.

misconceptions.description: Thinks the LCM of two numbers is always their product.
misconceptions.signal: Writes LCM(4, 6) = 24 without checking smaller common multiples.
misconceptions.remedy: List multiples of both numbers side by side and circle the first common one (12), then discuss when the product IS the LCM (only when the HCF is 1).

misconceptions.description: Misapplies divisibility tests, e.g. 'a number ending in 3 is divisible by 3'.
misconceptions.signal: Checks only the last digit for divisibility by 3 or 9.
misconceptions.remedy: Sort the tests into two families — last-digit tests (2, 5, 10) and digit-sum tests (3, 9) — and test conjectures on counterexamples like 13 and 23.

real_world_hooks: Two railway lines with trains every 8 and 12 minutes — when do trains arrive together? (LCM)
Cutting two ribbons of 12 m and 18 m into equal longest pieces with nothing left over (HCF)
Arranging 36 laddoos into equal rows for a festival tray — factor pairs

questions.prompt: Find the HCF of 12 and 18.

options.diagnosis: Found a common factor but stopped too early; did not check for a higher one.

questions.explanation: Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. Common factors are 1, 2, 3, 6 and the highest is 6. Note 36 is the LCM, and 216 = 12 × 18 is the product — neither is a factor of both numbers.

questions.prompt: Find the LCM of 4 and 6.

options.diagnosis: Added the two numbers instead of finding a common multiple.

questions.explanation: Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, … Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, … The lowest common multiple is 12. The product 24 is a common multiple, but not the lowest — because 4 and 6 share the factor 2.

questions.prompt: Two temple bells ring every 8 minutes and every 12 minutes. They ring together at 7:00 am. When do they next ring together?

options.diagnosis: Tracked only the 8-minute bell; 16 is not a multiple of 12, so the bells do not coincide then.

questions.explanation: The bells coincide at common multiples of 8 and 12. LCM(8, 12) = 24, so they next ring together 24 minutes later, at 7:24 am. The answer 7:04 uses the HCF (4), and 8:36 uses the product (96 minutes) — a common multiple, but not the next one.

nodes.title: Integers: Negative Numbers, Ordering, Addition and Subtraction
nodes.description: Integers extend the number line to the left of zero, letting us describe temperatures below freezing, depths below sea level and money owed. You will order integers, and add and subtract them using the number line and zero-pair models — the foundation for all of algebra.
learning_outcomes: Can represent real situations (temperature, altitude, credit/debit) with positive and negative integers
Can place integers on a number line and compare/order them correctly
Can add integers with like and unlike signs using number-line moves or zero pairs
Can subtract integers, including subtracting a negative, and explain why 5 − (−2) = 7

misconceptions.description: Orders negative numbers by magnitude: thinks −5 > −3 because 5 > 3.
misconceptions.signal: Says −7°C is warmer than −2°C, or places −5 to the right of −3 on the number line.
misconceptions.remedy: Use a vertical thermometer or lift model: 'lower floor = smaller number'. Repeatedly ask 'which is further LEFT (or lower)?' rather than 'which looks bigger?', until left-means-less is automatic.

misconceptions.description: Drops or ignores signs when computing, adding magnitudes as if all numbers were positive (e.g. −3 + (−4) = 7).
misconceptions.signal: Answers with the right magnitude but wrong or missing sign; treats −3 + (−4) like 3 + 4.
misconceptions.remedy: Model with coloured counters: 3 red (negative) counters plus 4 red counters gives 7 RED counters, i.e. −7. Have the student state the sign of the answer before computing the magnitude.

misconceptions.description: Treats subtracting a negative as the same as subtracting a positive: 5 − (−2) = 3.
misconceptions.signal: Ignores the second minus sign, or says 'two minuses is still minus' for subtraction.
misconceptions.remedy: Use the debt-cancellation story: removing a ₹2 debt makes you ₹2 richer. On the number line, show that subtracting a number means facing the opposite direction of that number's sign, so 5 − (−2) moves right to 7.

misconceptions.description: Believes you cannot subtract a bigger number from a smaller one.
misconceptions.signal: Declares 3 − 7 'impossible' or silently flips it to 7 − 3 = 4.
misconceptions.remedy: Play a points game where scores genuinely go below zero (lose 7 points while on 3). Show 3 − 7 on the number line landing at −4, and contrast the answers 3 − 7 = −4 and 7 − 3 = 4 side by side.

real_world_hooks: Winter temperatures: Srinagar at −4°C vs Delhi at 8°C — who is colder, and by how much?
Bank/UPI balance: spending more than you have and seeing a negative balance
Lift buttons: basement floors B1, B2 as −1, −2; sea level and submarines

questions.prompt: Compute: (−3) + (−4)

options.diagnosis: Found the difference 4 − 3 instead of the sum; mixing up the unlike-signs rule with the like-signs case.
Multiplied instead of adding.

questions.explanation: Both numbers are negative, so we combine the debts: 3 below zero and 4 more below zero is 7 below zero. (−3) + (−4) = −7. The magnitudes add; the shared negative sign stays.

questions.prompt: Compute: 5 − (−2)

options.diagnosis: Sign confusion: computed the correct magnitude but negated the result.
Multiplied 5 × 2 instead of subtracting.

questions.explanation: Subtracting a negative is the same as adding the positive: 5 − (−2) = 5 + 2 = 7. Think of removing a ₹2 debt from your account — you end up ₹2 better off, not worse.

questions.prompt: At night the temperature in Leh was −4°C. By noon it had RISEN by 7°C. What was the temperature at noon?

options.diagnosis: Subtracted 7 instead of adding; 'rose by 7' means move UP the thermometer.
Correct magnitude but wrong sign; likely lost track of which side of zero the answer landed on.

questions.explanation: Start at −4 and move up 7: −4 + 7 = 3. On the thermometer you pass −3, −2, −1, 0, then 1, 2, 3. Adding the magnitudes (4 + 7 = 11) is wrong because the temperature starts below zero and the rise first has to 'pay off' those 4 degrees.

nodes.title: Fractions: Proper, Improper, Mixed; Addition and Subtraction
nodes.description: You will work confidently with proper fractions, improper fractions and mixed numbers, convert between forms, and add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators using equivalent fractions and the LCM. This is where fraction arithmetic becomes a reliable tool instead of a guessing game.
learning_outcomes: Can convert between improper fractions and mixed numbers in both directions
Can compare fractions by making denominators (or numerators) equal
Can add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators using the LCM as common denominator
Can solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions and judge whether the answer is reasonable

misconceptions.description: Adds (or subtracts) fractions by combining numerators and denominators separately: 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5.
misconceptions.signal: Writes a/b + c/d = (a+c)/(b+d); the 'answer' is often smaller than one of the fractions being added.
misconceptions.remedy: Show the contradiction concretely: 1/2 + 1/3 must be MORE than 1/2, but 2/5 is less. Then rebuild addition with fraction strips — only same-sized pieces can be counted together, which is why we first make denominators equal.

misconceptions.description: Believes a bigger denominator means a bigger fraction (1/8 > 1/4 because 8 > 4).
misconceptions.signal: Orders unit fractions the same way as whole numbers.
misconceptions.remedy: Cut the same roti into 4 parts and into 8 parts: more pieces means each piece is smaller. Practise ordering unit fractions on a number line until 'bigger denominator, smaller piece' is internalised.

misconceptions.description: Reads a mixed number as multiplication: thinks 2¾ means 2 × ¾.
misconceptions.signal: Converts 2¾ to 6/4, or evaluates it as 1.5.
misconceptions.remedy: Expand the notation aloud every time: 2¾ = 2 + ¾, 'two wholes AND three quarters'. Show it on a number line between 2 and 3, then derive the improper form 11/4 from 8/4 + 3/4.

misconceptions.description: Thinks improper fractions like 7/4 are 'wrong' or impossible because the numerator exceeds the denominator.
misconceptions.signal: Refuses to write 7/4, or 'corrects' it to 4/7.
misconceptions.remedy: Pour 7 quarter-cups of water: it is simply more than one cup. Place 7/4 on the number line at 1¾ and practise moving fluently between the improper and mixed forms.

real_world_hooks: Sharing pizzas or parathas: 3 parathas among 4 people each
Recipe scaling: ¾ cup sugar when you only have a ¼-cup measure
Cricket: bowling 3½ overs — a mixed number in the scorecard

questions.prompt: Compute: 3/8 + 2/8

options.diagnosis: Subtracted the numerators instead of adding.
Multiplied the numerators (3 × 2) while keeping the denominator.

questions.explanation: The pieces are already the same size (eighths), so just count them: 3 eighths + 2 eighths = 5 eighths = 5/8. The denominator names the piece size and does not get added.

questions.prompt: Compute: 1/2 + 1/3

options.diagnosis: Found the common denominator 6 but forgot to convert the numerators before adding.
Multiplied the fractions instead of adding them.

questions.explanation: LCM of 2 and 3 is 6. Convert: 1/2 = 3/6 and 1/3 = 2/6. Then 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6. Sanity check: the answer must be bigger than 1/2, and 5/6 is — while 2/5 is not.

questions.prompt: A recipe needs 3/4 cup of sugar. Asha has only 1/2 cup. How much more sugar does she need?

options.diagnosis: Subtracted numerators over the first denominator (3−1)/4 without first converting 1/2 to 2/4.
Added the fractions instead of finding the difference.

questions.explanation: Needed − has = 3/4 − 1/2. Convert 1/2 to 2/4, then 3/4 − 2/4 = 1/4 cup. The answer '1 cup' comes from subtracting tops and bottoms separately: (3−1)/(4−2) = 2/2 — but needing MORE than the whole recipe's sugar makes no sense.

nodes.title: Decimals: Comparing, Adding, Subtracting; Units
nodes.description: Decimals are fractions with denominators 10, 100, 1000 written in place-value form. You will compare decimals correctly, add and subtract them by aligning the decimal point, and use them with money and metric units — where decimals live in real life.
learning_outcomes: Can read and write decimals up to thousandths and connect them to fractions
Can compare and order decimals by place value, including cases like 0.5 vs 0.45
Can add and subtract decimals by aligning decimal points, padding with zeros where needed
Can convert between units using decimals (e.g. 145 cm = 1.45 m, 75 paise = ₹0.75)

misconceptions.description: 'Longer is larger': treats the digits after the point as a whole number, so 0.45 > 0.5 because 45 > 5.
misconceptions.signal: Ranks decimals by counting digits or comparing the 'decimal part' as a whole number.
misconceptions.remedy: Pad to equal lengths (0.50 vs 0.45) so place values line up, and verify on a number line or with money: ₹0.50 is 50 paise, ₹0.45 is 45 paise.

misconceptions.description: Adds/subtracts decimals by right-aligning digits like whole numbers instead of aligning the decimal points.
misconceptions.signal: Computes 12.5 + 3.75 as 125 + 375 = 500 and writes 5.00 or similar.
misconceptions.remedy: Use squared paper with a drawn vertical line for the decimal point; require padding with zeros (12.50 + 3.75) before adding, and estimate first (12 + 4 ≈ 16) to catch absurd answers.

misconceptions.description: Thinks 0.7 and 0.70 are different numbers (0.70 seen as bigger 'because it has more digits').
misconceptions.signal: Refuses to accept 0.7 = 0.70, or treats trailing zeros as changing the value.
misconceptions.remedy: Show both as fractions: 7/10 = 70/100 via equivalent fractions, and as money: ₹0.7 of a rupee is the same 70 paise as ₹0.70.

misconceptions.description: Slides the decimal point incorrectly when converting units (e.g. 5 paise = ₹0.5, or 45 cm = 4.5 m).
misconceptions.signal: Off-by-one-place answers in money and metric conversions.
misconceptions.remedy: Anchor the conversion factors explicitly (100 paise = ₹1, 100 cm = 1 m, 1000 m = 1 km) and always write the division: 45 cm = 45/100 m = 0.45 m.

real_world_hooks: Petrol price boards: ₹104.85 per litre — reading and comparing decimals daily
Athletics timings: 10.09 s vs 10.5 s — who won the race?
Shop bills and UPI amounts: adding ₹12.50 and ₹3.75
teaching.video_search: comparing adding subtracting decimals place value class 6

questions.prompt: Which statement is TRUE?

options.diagnosis: Place-value confusion: tenths and hundredths treated as interchangeable.

questions.explanation: Pad to the same length: 0.5 = 0.50. Comparing 0.50 with 0.45 place by place, 5 tenths beats 4 tenths, so 0.5 > 0.45. Trailing zeros after the decimal point change nothing: 0.50 = 0.5.

questions.prompt: Compute: 12.5 + 3.75

options.diagnosis: Aligned correctly but dropped the carry from 0.5 + 0.75 = 1.25.
Padded 12.5 as 12.05 instead of 12.50 — the zero went to the wrong side.

questions.explanation: Align the decimal points and pad: 12.50 + 3.75. Hundredths: 0+5=5. Tenths: 5+7=12, write 2 carry 1. Ones: 2+3+1=6. Tens: 1. Answer: 16.25. Estimate check: 12 + 4 ≈ 16 ✓.

questions.prompt: A rope is 15 m long. Two pieces of lengths 3.65 m and 4.5 m are cut off. How much rope remains?

options.diagnosis: Borrowing error while subtracting 8.15 from 15.00.
Subtracted only the first piece; forgot the 4.5 m cut.

questions.explanation: Total cut = 3.65 + 4.50 = 8.15 m. Remaining = 15.00 − 8.15 = 6.85 m. The answer 10.90 comes from right-aligning 3.65 and 4.5 as whole numbers (365 + 45 = 410 → 4.10) — aligning the decimal points prevents this.

nodes.title: Ratio, Proportion and the Unitary Method
nodes.description: A ratio compares quantities by division rather than subtraction, and a proportion says two ratios are equal. With the unitary method — find the value of ONE, then scale — you can solve price, speed and recipe problems. This multiplicative way of thinking underpins percentages, similar triangles and trigonometry later.
learning_outcomes: Can express a comparison as a ratio in simplest form, attending to order and same units
Can test whether four numbers are in proportion (a:b = c:d)
Can use the unitary method: find the value of one unit, then find the value of many
Can solve real problems on prices, speeds and mixtures using ratio reasoning

misconceptions.description: Uses additive instead of multiplicative reasoning: compares by subtracting ('10 and 15 differ by 5') or extends a ratio by adding the same amount to both parts.
misconceptions.signal: Answers ratio questions with a difference, or scales a recipe by adding 2 to every ingredient.
misconceptions.remedy: Contrast the two models on a doubling problem: if 2 cups rice serve 4 people, 4 cups serve 8 (not 6). Use double number lines so scaling is seen as stretching, not shifting.

misconceptions.description: Thinks the order in a ratio doesn't matter: 2:3 is the same as 3:2.
misconceptions.signal: Writes the numbers in either order and treats the answers as interchangeable.
misconceptions.remedy: Use contexts where the swap is obviously wrong (ratio of sugar to salt in a recipe!). Insist on labelling each part of the ratio in words before writing numbers.

misconceptions.description: Confuses part-to-part with part-to-whole ratios (pens:pencils vs pens:total).
misconceptions.signal: Given 10 pens and 15 pencils, writes the pens ratio as 10:25 or as 2:3 of the total interchangeably.
misconceptions.remedy: Draw bar models splitting the whole into labelled parts; always ask 'compared to WHAT?' before writing the ratio.

misconceptions.description: In the unitary method, multiplies where division is needed (or inverts the proportion), e.g. fewer items should cost less but the calculation gives more.
misconceptions.signal: Sets up 6 notebooks → ₹90, 10 notebooks → 90 × 6 ÷ 10.
misconceptions.remedy: Force the middle step in words: 'ONE notebook costs 90 ÷ 6 = ₹15.' Then predict the direction (more notebooks → more money) and check the answer against the prediction.

real_world_hooks: Cricket run rate: 48 runs in 6 overs — runs per over, and projecting a total
Comparing prices: which pack of biscuits is the better deal per rupee?
Scaling a recipe for guests: chai for 2 vs chai for 7
Map scales: 1 cm on the map = 5 km on the ground
teaching.video_search: ratio proportion unitary method word problems class 6

questions.prompt: A box has 10 pens and 15 pencils. What is the ratio of pens to pencils in simplest form?
questions.explanation: Pens : pencils = 10 : 15. Divide both by their HCF 5 to get 2 : 3. Order matters — 3:2 would be pencils to pens. And 2:5 compares pens to the TOTAL of 25 items, which is a different question. '5' is just the difference, not a ratio.

questions.prompt: 6 notebooks cost ₹90. What do 10 such notebooks cost?

options.diagnosis: Multiplied 90 × 6 instead of first dividing to find the cost of one notebook.

questions.explanation: Unitary method: one notebook costs 90 ÷ 6 = ₹15, so 10 cost 15 × 10 = ₹150. Direction check: more notebooks must cost more than ₹90 — which rules out ₹54. ₹94 comes from adding the extra 4 notebooks as ₹1 each, an additive error.

questions.prompt: A car travels 240 km on 16 litres of petrol. How much petrol is needed for a 600 km trip at the same rate?

options.diagnosis: Computed 600 ÷ 16, dividing distance by litres of the OLD trip — mixed up which rate to use.

questions.explanation: Mileage = 240 ÷ 16 = 15 km per litre. Petrol needed = 600 ÷ 15 = 40 litres. Check: 600 km is 2.5 times 240 km, and 2.5 × 16 = 40 ✓. The additive answer 376 (16 + the extra 360 km) treats kilometres as if they were litres.

nodes.title: Introduction to Algebra: Variables and Expressions
nodes.description: Algebra begins when a letter stands for a number that can vary. You will write rules for patterns (like the perimeter of a square, 4s), build expressions from operations, and evaluate them for given values. Learning to treat a letter as a NUMBER — not an object or a label — is the single most important idea of this chapter.
learning_outcomes: Can use a variable to state a general rule for a pattern (e.g. matchstick patterns, perimeter formulas)
Can translate word phrases into algebraic expressions and back
Can evaluate an expression like 2n + 3 for a given value of n
Can explain that a variable stands for a number that can take many values

misconceptions.description: Treats a letter as a label or object ('3a means 3 apples') rather than as a number.
misconceptions.signal: Reads 3a as 'three apples', or refuses to compute with letters because 'they aren't numbers'.
misconceptions.remedy: Use function-machine games: n goes in, 3n comes out, for MANY values of n. Repeatedly verbalise '3a means 3 times whatever number a is'.

misconceptions.description: Believes a variable stands for exactly one specific hidden number in all contexts.
misconceptions.signal: Asks 'but what IS x?' for an identity like n + n = 2n, or objects when x takes different values in different problems.
misconceptions.remedy: Tabulate n + n and 2n for n = 1, 2, 3, 10, 100 to show the rule holds for EVERY value; contrast a formula (always true) with an equation (true for particular values).

misconceptions.description: Conjoins terms: writes 3 + x as 3x, or treats 2n as the two-digit number '2 then n'.
misconceptions.signal: Simplifies 3 + x to 3x, or evaluates 2n at n = 5 as 25.
misconceptions.remedy: Substitute a number to expose the error: at x = 4, 3 + x = 7 but 3x = 12. Stress that placing a number next to a letter always means multiplication, never digit-joining.

misconceptions.description: Assigns letters values from their alphabet position (a = 1, b = 2, …).
misconceptions.signal: Evaluates expressions without being given values, using a = 1, b = 2, etc.
misconceptions.remedy: Deliberately assign 'wrong-order' values (let a = 7, b = 2) in exercises, and discuss that letter choice is arbitrary — the same rule could use n, t or ★.

real_world_hooks: Matchstick patterns: how many sticks for n squares in a row? (3n + 1)
Auto-rickshaw fare: ₹25 plus ₹12 per km — writing 25 + 12k
Age puzzles: 'my mother is 4 more than twice my age'
Mobile data plans: fixed cost plus cost per GB
teaching.video_search: introduction to algebra variables expressions matchstick patterns class 6

questions.prompt: The side of a square is s cm. Which expression gives its perimeter?

options.diagnosis: Counted only two of the four sides.

questions.explanation: The perimeter is s + s + s + s, one for each side, which is 4 × s = 4s. Note that s + 4 ADDS 4 instead of taking 4 copies, and the bare '4' ignores the side length entirely — the perimeter must change when s changes.

questions.prompt: If n = 5, what is the value of 2n + 3?

options.diagnosis: Added first, then multiplied: 2 × (5 + 3). Order of operations slip.
Computed 2n but forgot to add the 3.

questions.explanation: 2n means 2 × n = 2 × 5 = 10, then add 3 to get 13. The answer 28 comes from reading 2n as the digits '25' — but a number written next to a letter always means multiplication.

questions.prompt: Ritu is x years old. Her mother's age is 4 more than twice Ritu's age. Which expression gives the mother's age?

options.diagnosis: Swapped the roles of the two numbers: 'twice' must multiply x, and '4 more' must be added.
Sign slip: '4 more than' means add 4, not subtract.

questions.explanation: 'Twice Ritu's age' is 2x; '4 more than' that is 2x + 4. Check with a number: if Ritu is 10, mother is 2(10) + 4 = 24. Combining 2x and 4 into 6x is illegal — one is x's, the other is plain years.

nodes.title: Basic Geometrical Ideas: Points, Lines, Curves, Polygons, Circles
nodes.description: Geometry's vocabulary starts here: points, line segments, rays and lines; open and closed curves; polygons with their sides, vertices and diagonals; and the circle with its centre, radius, diameter and chords. Precise language now makes every later theorem readable.
learning_outcomes: Can distinguish a line, a line segment and a ray, and use correct notation for each
Can identify open/closed curves, and the interior, boundary and exterior of a closed curve
Can name the parts of a polygon (sides, vertices, adjacent sides, diagonals)
Can identify centre, radius, diameter, chord, arc and sector of a circle and relate diameter to radius

misconceptions.description: Thinks a line has endpoints and a definite length, confusing 'line' with 'line segment'.
misconceptions.signal: Asks for the length of line AB, or draws a line without arrowheads and calls it a line.
misconceptions.remedy: Use the torch-beam analogy (segment = stick, ray = torch beam, line = laser extending both ways forever) and insist on arrowhead conventions in every sketch.

misconceptions.description: Confuses radius and diameter, e.g. thinks the radius stretches all the way across the circle.
misconceptions.signal: Measures across the circle and calls it the radius, or says diameter = radius.
misconceptions.remedy: Fold a paper circle: a full fold-line through the centre is a diameter; half of it, centre to edge, is a radius. Derive and rehearse d = 2r with the folds in hand.

misconceptions.description: Thinks any closed figure is a polygon, including curved shapes like circles and ovals.
misconceptions.signal: Lists the circle among polygons, or accepts shapes with curved edges as polygons.
misconceptions.remedy: Sort a deck of shape cards into polygon/not-polygon and extract the definition: closed figure made ONLY of straight line segments.

misconceptions.description: Judges lines parallel or intersecting only by the drawn picture: if segments don't touch on the page, they 'don't intersect'.
misconceptions.signal: Says two non-parallel segments are parallel because their drawn portions don't meet.
misconceptions.remedy: Extend the drawings with a ruler beyond the page edge; discuss that lines go on forever, so intersection depends on direction, not on the visible part.

real_world_hooks: Railway tracks and level crossings: parallel and intersecting lines
A cycle wheel: spokes as radii, the rim as the circle
Rangoli and kolam designs: closed curves, interiors and boundaries
Roads on a city map: segments, intersections and curves
teaching.video_search: basic geometrical ideas points lines rays polygons circle parts class 6

questions.prompt: Which of these has exactly TWO endpoints?

options.diagnosis: Partial understanding: a ray has exactly one endpoint and extends forever the other way.
Word-association with 'endpoint'; a point has no length at all and no endpoints.

questions.explanation: A line segment is the portion between two endpoints — it has definite length. A line extends without end in both directions (no endpoints); a ray has one endpoint and extends forever in one direction.

questions.prompt: A circle has radius 6 cm. What is its diameter?

options.diagnosis: Inverted the relationship: halved instead of doubling.
Squared the radius — mixing in a half-remembered area formula.

questions.explanation: A diameter passes through the centre from edge to edge, so it is two radii end to end: d = 2r = 2 × 6 = 12 cm.

questions.prompt: Two DIFFERENT lines are drawn in a plane. In how many points can they intersect, at most?

options.diagnosis: Thinking of curves (like a circle and a line); two straight lines cannot cross, separate, and cross again.
That happens only when the two 'lines' are actually the same line — but the question says they are different.

questions.explanation: Two distinct straight lines either never meet (parallel) or cross at exactly one point. They can never meet twice: through two different points there is only ONE line, so meeting twice would force them to be the same line.

nodes.title: Understanding Elementary Shapes: Angles, Triangles, Quadrilaterals, Solids
nodes.description: You will measure and classify angles (acute, right, obtuse, straight, reflex), classify triangles by sides and angles, meet the family of quadrilaterals, and recognise common solids with their faces, edges and vertices. Classifying shapes trains you to reason from properties rather than appearances.
learning_outcomes: Can classify angles as acute, right, obtuse, straight or reflex, and estimate angle sizes
Can classify triangles by sides (scalene, isosceles, equilateral) and by angles (acute, right, obtuse)
Can name quadrilaterals and state their defining properties, including how the special quadrilaterals nest (every square is a rectangle)
Can identify faces, edges and vertices of cubes, cuboids, cylinders, cones, spheres, prisms and pyramids

misconceptions.description: Thinks an angle is bigger when its arms are drawn longer, confusing arm length with the amount of turn.
misconceptions.signal: Says a 30° angle with long arms is larger than a 60° angle with short arms.
misconceptions.remedy: Use two card strips joined by a split pin: opening the 'jaws' changes the angle, trimming the strips does not. Overlay traced angles at a shared vertex to compare turn directly.

misconceptions.description: Treats triangle categories as exclusive: an equilateral triangle 'cannot' be isosceles, or one unequal side makes a triangle scalene.
misconceptions.signal: Classifies a 5-5-8 triangle as scalene 'because one side is different', or objects that equilateral triangles satisfy the isosceles definition.
misconceptions.remedy: Work from the definitions as minimum conditions ('AT LEAST two equal sides') and sort triangles into overlapping circles (Venn diagram) rather than separate boxes.

misconceptions.description: Mixes up the labels acute/obtuse/right, or calls any 'corner' a right angle.
misconceptions.signal: Labels a 120° angle acute, or calls every corner of every shape a right angle.
misconceptions.remedy: Give a personal benchmark: the corner of a notebook page is exactly 90°. Physically test angles against the page corner and sort them into smaller-than / equal / bigger-than piles before naming.

misconceptions.description: Believes a square is not a rectangle (categories judged by appearance, not properties).
misconceptions.signal: Insists 'that's a square, not a rectangle', or says a tilted square is 'a diamond, not a square'.
misconceptions.remedy: Check the rectangle's property list (four right angles, opposite sides equal) against a square — it passes every test. Rotate cutouts to show orientation does not change what a shape is.

real_world_hooks: Clock hands: what angle do they make at 3:00, 4:00, 6:00?
Opening a laptop or door: watching an angle grow from acute to obtuse
Road signs: triangles and their types; kite-flying and quadrilaterals
Cartons and cans in a kirana shop: cuboids and cylinders, counting faces and edges
teaching.video_search: types of angles triangles quadrilaterals classification class 6

questions.prompt: An angle measuring 120° is called:

options.diagnosis: Boundary error: reflex angles are those bigger than 180°, not 90°.

questions.explanation: Compare with 90°: an angle between 90° and 180° is obtuse. Acute means less than 90°, right means exactly 90°, and reflex means more than 180° (up to 360°). 120° sits between 90° and 180°, so it is obtuse.

questions.prompt: A triangle has sides 5 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm. It is best classified as:

options.diagnosis: Saw two equal sides and over-generalised; equilateral needs all THREE sides equal.
Guessed from the numbers; check 5² + 5² = 50 ≠ 64 = 8², so there is no right angle.

questions.explanation: Two sides are equal (5 and 5), so the triangle is isosceles. Scalene means ALL sides different; equilateral means all sides equal. The angle classification is separate — this one is actually obtuse, not right-angled, since 5² + 5² < 8².

questions.prompt: Which statement is TRUE?

options.text: A square is a rectangle only when it is drawn with horizontal sides
options.diagnosis: Orientation-dependence: what a shape IS cannot change when you rotate the page.

questions.explanation: A rectangle is a quadrilateral with four right angles. A square has four right angles (and, additionally, four equal sides), so every square passes the rectangle test. The reverse fails: a 3×5 rectangle has unequal adjacent sides, so it is not a square.

nodes.title: Symmetry: Lines of Symmetry
nodes.description: A figure has line symmetry when one half folds exactly onto the other. You will find all lines of symmetry of common shapes and letters, and complete half-drawn symmetric figures. Symmetry sharpens visual reasoning and reappears in reflections, transformations and even algebraic graphs.
learning_outcomes: Can test a proposed line of symmetry by (mentally or physically) folding
Can find ALL lines of symmetry of standard shapes: square (4), rectangle (2), equilateral triangle (3), circle (infinitely many)
Can identify shapes with no line of symmetry (e.g. scalene triangle, parallelogram)
Can complete the other half of a figure given the mirror line

misconceptions.description: Thinks the diagonal of a rectangle is a line of symmetry.
misconceptions.signal: Claims a (non-square) rectangle has 4 lines of symmetry, counting both diagonals.
misconceptions.remedy: Actually fold a rectangular sheet along its diagonal — the two halves visibly do not match (they overhang). Contrast with the square, where the diagonal fold works because all sides are equal.

misconceptions.description: Believes every shape must have at least one line of symmetry.
misconceptions.signal: Keeps hunting for a mirror line on a scalene triangle or parallelogram and 'finds' a wrong one rather than answering zero.
misconceptions.remedy: Give a sorting task that includes genuinely asymmetric shapes, and make 'zero lines of symmetry' an explicitly allowed, checkable answer via folding.

misconceptions.description: Only recognises vertical mirror lines; misses horizontal and slanted ones.
misconceptions.signal: Says B has no line of symmetry (its line is horizontal), or finds only 1 of the square's 4 lines.
misconceptions.remedy: Rotate the figure (or the student's page!) while testing folds, and use a small mirror placed at different orientations to hunt systematically: vertical, horizontal, then diagonals.

misconceptions.description: Assumes the number of lines of symmetry always equals the number of sides.
misconceptions.signal: Answers '4' for any quadrilateral and '3' for any triangle without checking.
misconceptions.remedy: Test the rule against a parallelogram (4 sides, 0 lines) and a scalene triangle (3 sides, 0 lines); refine to: the rule holds only for REGULAR polygons.

real_world_hooks: Rangoli, mehndi and Taj Mahal photos: hunting mirror lines in Indian design
Cutting symmetric shapes from folded paper, like festival decorations
Letters and logos: which alphabets and brand marks are symmetric?
Butterfly wings and human faces: how symmetric are they really?
teaching.video_search: lines of symmetry shapes folding test class 6

questions.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?

options.diagnosis: Double-counted: each fold line was counted once per half.

questions.explanation: A square has 4 lines of symmetry: the vertical line, the horizontal line, and BOTH diagonals. Students who find only 2 usually miss the diagonal folds — try them on a paper square.

questions.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a rectangle (that is not a square) have?

options.diagnosis: Over-correction: the two 'midline' folds do work, even though the diagonal folds fail.

questions.explanation: The two lines joining midpoints of opposite sides are lines of symmetry. The diagonals are NOT: folding along a diagonal leaves overhanging corners because adjacent sides have different lengths. So the count is 2, not 4.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a line of symmetry of a rectangle?

options.text: The line joining the midpoints of two opposite sides
Any line passing through its centre
options.diagnosis: Over-generalising from the circle; for a rectangle only two special lines through the centre work.

options.text: The line joining the midpoints of two ADJACENT sides
options.diagnosis: This cuts off a corner; folding along it clearly does not map the rectangle onto itself.

questions.explanation: Folding along the line through midpoints of opposite sides matches the two halves exactly. A diagonal fold fails (unequal adjacent sides), and most other lines through the centre give half-turn symmetry, not mirror symmetry.

nodes.title: Constructions with Ruler and Compass
nodes.description: Using only an unmarked straightedge and a compass, you will construct circles, copy segments, draw perpendiculars and perpendicular bisectors, and build angles of 60°, 30°, 90° and 120°. Constructions teach WHY figures have their properties — every arc is a statement about equal distances.
learning_outcomes: Can draw a circle of given radius and copy a line segment with compass and ruler
Can construct the perpendicular bisector of a segment and a perpendicular through a point
Can construct 60° and related angles (120°, 30°, 90°) and bisect a given angle
Can explain why a construction works in terms of equal radii (equal distances)

misconceptions.description: Thinks measuring with a protractor or marked ruler counts as 'construction', or that constructions are just careful drawing tricks with no reasoning behind them.
misconceptions.signal: Reaches for the protractor to 'construct' a 60° angle; cannot say why the compass method gives exactly 60°.
misconceptions.remedy: Reveal the hidden equilateral triangle: join the arc intersection points and measure the three equal sides. Constructions become logical arguments (equal radii ⇒ equal sides ⇒ 60°), not rituals.

misconceptions.description: Lets the compass width drift mid-construction, believing the radius doesn't need to stay fixed.
misconceptions.signal: Arcs that should intersect don't; bisectors come out visibly off-centre; the student shrugs and adjusts by eye.
misconceptions.remedy: Demonstrate a deliberate 'sabotaged' construction with changed radius and compare with a correct one. Teach the physical skills: tighten the hinge, hold by the handle, lean the compass in the direction of turn.

misconceptions.description: Thinks the perpendicular bisector is just any line through the midpoint (perpendicularity ignored), or just the midpoint itself.
misconceptions.signal: Marks the midpoint with a ruler and draws a slanted line through it, calling it the perpendicular bisector.
misconceptions.remedy: Emphasise both conditions with a checklist (passes through midpoint ✓, makes 90° ✓) and show that the equal-arcs construction guarantees both at once.

misconceptions.description: Believes the size of the arcs (compass opening) chosen during bisection changes the answer, so there is 'one right opening'.
misconceptions.signal: Asks 'how much should I open the compass?' expecting a specific number; erases work when a different opening is used.
misconceptions.remedy: Have the student bisect the same angle three times with three different openings on tracing paper and overlay the results — the bisector lands in the same place every time (as long as the opening stays fixed WITHIN one step).

real_world_hooks: How a carpenter marks a perpendicular cut with just string and a pencil
Drawing a perfect circle for a cricket pitch or rangoli using a rope as compass
Finding the exact middle of a doorway or shelf without measuring numbers
teaching.video_search: ruler compass constructions perpendicular bisector 60 degree angle class 6

questions.prompt: To draw a circle of radius 4 cm, you should open the compass to:

options.diagnosis: Confused radius with diameter; the compass opening is the centre-to-edge distance.
Halved the radius, perhaps thinking the opening spans only half way.

options.text: Any width — you can adjust it while drawing

questions.explanation: The compass opening IS the radius: every point of the circle sits exactly that distance from the centre. Open it to 4 cm on the ruler and keep it fixed while you turn — changing it mid-turn breaks the equal-distance property that makes it a circle.

questions.prompt: In the compass construction of a 60° angle, why does the angle come out exactly 60°?

options.text: The two arcs and the base segment create an equilateral triangle, and each angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°
Compasses are manufactured to draw 60° automatically
Because the first arc must be drawn exactly 6 cm wide
It is only approximately 60°; you fix it with a protractor afterwards

questions.explanation: Keeping the same compass opening makes three equal lengths: the base and the two arc radii. Equal sides force an equilateral triangle, whose angles are all 60°. The opening's actual size never matters — only that it stays the SAME.

questions.prompt: P is a point on the perpendicular bisector of segment AB. What must be true about P?

options.text: P is equidistant from A and B
P must be the midpoint of AB
P is at distance exactly AB from both A and B
options.diagnosis: Confuses 'equal distances' with one specific distance; points on the bisector are at ALL sorts of (equal) distances.

options.text: P is always closer to A than to B
options.diagnosis: Misses the symmetry entirely; the bisector is precisely the set of points that favour neither end.

questions.explanation: The perpendicular bisector is exactly the set of points equally far from A and B. The midpoint is just one such point — every other point on the line is also equidistant (that's why the equal-arc construction, which marks two points equidistant from A and B, produces this line).

nodes.title: Mensuration: Perimeter and Area of Squares and Rectangles
nodes.description: Perimeter measures the boundary of a figure; area measures the surface it covers. You will use the formulas for squares and rectangles, work with the right units (cm vs cm²), and discover that figures with the same perimeter can enclose very different areas.
learning_outcomes: Can compute perimeters of rectangles, squares and figures made of straight segments
Can compute areas of rectangles and squares, and of shapes decomposable into rectangles
Can attach correct units: linear units for perimeter, square units for area
Can explain with examples that equal perimeters do not force equal areas (and vice versa)

misconceptions.description: Confuses area and perimeter — uses the wrong formula or swaps the two concepts.
misconceptions.signal: Answers 'area 26 cm' for an 8×5 rectangle, or multiplies sides when asked for the boundary length.
misconceptions.remedy: Tie each to a physical action: perimeter = walking the fence (add the walk), area = counting the tiles inside (multiply rows × columns). Have the student state WHICH action the problem asks for before computing.

misconceptions.description: Believes shapes with the same perimeter must have the same area (and same area forces same perimeter).
misconceptions.signal: Argues a 6×4 and an 8×2 rectangle 'must' have equal areas since both use 20 cm of boundary.
misconceptions.remedy: Give a fixed 20 cm loop of string on squared paper and record the areas of different rectangles it can bound (1×9 = 9 up to 5×5 = 25). The table itself refutes the belief memorably.

misconceptions.description: Writes area in linear units (cm) or perimeter in square units (cm²), treating units as decoration.
misconceptions.signal: Answers '49 cm' for the area of a 7 cm square.
misconceptions.remedy: Show that area counts unit SQUARES: each tile is 1 cm × 1 cm = 1 cm². Make unit-checking a final step of every answer: 'did I count steps (cm) or tiles (cm²)?'

misconceptions.description: Computes a rectangle's perimeter as just length + breadth, forgetting the figure has four sides.
misconceptions.signal: Gives 13 cm for the perimeter of an 8×5 rectangle.
misconceptions.remedy: Trace the full boundary with a finger, counting all four sides aloud: 8 + 5 + 8 + 5. Then compress the reasoning into the formula 2 × (l + b) so the doubling is understood, not memorised.

real_world_hooks: Fencing a vegetable patch vs buying grass to cover it — one is perimeter, the other area
Tiling a bathroom floor: how many 1-ft tiles for a 6 ft × 8 ft floor?
Photo frames (border) vs the photo itself (surface)
Boundary rope for a school sports ground
teaching.video_search: perimeter and area of rectangle square word problems class 6

questions.prompt: Find the perimeter of a rectangle with length 8 cm and breadth 5 cm.

options.diagnosis: Used 4 × 5, applying the square's perimeter formula to one side only.

questions.explanation: Perimeter = walk all four sides: 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 2 × (8 + 5) = 26 cm. Multiplying 8 × 5 = 40 gives the AREA (in cm², not cm) — a different question entirely.

questions.prompt: What is the area of a square of side 7 cm?

options.diagnosis: Added two sides (7 + 7) instead of multiplying side × side.

questions.explanation: Area = side × side = 7 × 7 = 49, and since we are counting 1 cm × 1 cm tiles, the unit is cm². Note 28 cm is the perimeter (4 × 7). The number 49 with unit 'cm' is wrong too — area is measured in square units.

questions.prompt: Rectangle A is 6 cm × 4 cm and rectangle B is 8 cm × 2 cm. Both have perimeter 20 cm. Do they have the same area?

options.text: No — A has area 24 cm² and B has area 16 cm²
Yes — same perimeter always means same area
It cannot be decided without drawing them
options.diagnosis: The formulas decide it exactly; measurement or drawing is not needed.

questions.explanation: Area A = 6 × 4 = 24 cm²; Area B = 8 × 2 = 16 cm². Equal perimeters, different areas: the same boundary length encloses more area the closer the rectangle is to a square. Perimeter and area measure genuinely different things.

nodes.title: Data Handling: Tally Marks, Pictographs, Bar Graphs
nodes.description: Data becomes useful when organised: you will record data with tally marks, and read and draw pictographs and bar graphs — including ones where a symbol or one unit of height stands for many items. Reading scales correctly is the key skill; it protects you from misleading graphs forever after.
learning_outcomes: Can record raw data in a frequency table using tally marks (bundles of five)
Can read and draw a pictograph where one symbol represents multiple units, including half symbols
Can read and draw a bar graph, choosing and using a sensible scale
Can answer comparison questions ('how many more…?') from a graph, applying the scale correctly

misconceptions.description: Miscounts tally bundles — treats the five-bar gate 卌 as 4 (or some other number of) strokes.
misconceptions.signal: Counts 卌 卌 || as 10 or 14 instead of 12.
misconceptions.remedy: Rebuild the convention physically: make four vertical strokes, then the diagonal 'gate' is the FIFTH. Practise skip-counting completed bundles by 5 before adding the loose strokes.

misconceptions.description: Ignores the scale of a bar graph, reading bar heights as raw counts (or comparing bars by grid squares only).
misconceptions.signal: Says 'this bar is 2 more' when it is 2 UNITS higher and each unit is 5, so the true gap is 10.
misconceptions.remedy: Always convert units to values at the axis before comparing: write the value at the top of each bar first. Show the same data drawn at two scales to prove the bars' look depends on scale.

misconceptions.description: Reads each pictograph symbol as one item even when the key says otherwise, and drops half symbols.
misconceptions.signal: Answers '3' or '4' for a row of 3½ symbols with key '1 symbol = 10 fans'.
misconceptions.remedy: Ritualise 'key first': circle the key before reading any row. Practise with keys of 2, 5, 10 and rows containing half symbols so multiplying by the key becomes automatic.

misconceptions.description: Answers 'how many more' questions by naming the bigger category or restating one value instead of finding the difference.
misconceptions.signal: Q: 'How many more students chose cricket than football?' A: 'Cricket' or the cricket total.
misconceptions.remedy: Model comparison as subtraction with the bars themselves: cover the common height of the two bars and count only the part that sticks out.

real_world_hooks: Class survey: favourite IPL team or favourite fruit, recorded live in tallies
Runs scored per over shown as a bar graph on TV — reading the scale
Vehicle count outside school for a traffic-safety project
Rainfall by month in your city as a pictograph
teaching.video_search: data handling tally marks pictograph bar graph scale class 6

questions.prompt: A tally record shows 卌 卌 || (two full bundles and two single strokes). What count does it represent?

options.diagnosis: Counted one bundle as 5 plus the 2 singles but overlooked the second bundle.

questions.explanation: Each full five-bar gate 卌 is 5 (four strokes plus the crossing fifth). So 5 + 5 + 2 = 12. Counting a bundle as 4 gives 10; treating each bundle as 10 gives 22 — both come from misreading the convention.

questions.prompt: In a pictograph, one fan symbol = 10 fans sold. Monday's row shows 3 full symbols and 1 half symbol. How many fans were sold on Monday?

options.diagnosis: Applied the key to full symbols but dropped the half symbol (worth 5).
Multiplied by 100 instead of 10 — scale slip.

questions.explanation: Key first: each symbol is 10 fans, so a half symbol is 5. Total = 3 × 10 + 5 = 35 fans. Counting symbols without the key ('about 4') answers a different, useless question.

questions.prompt: On a bar graph, 1 unit of height = 5 students. Cricket's bar is 6 units tall and football's bar is 4 units tall. How many MORE students chose cricket than football?

options.diagnosis: Added the two values (30 + 20) instead of subtracting.

questions.explanation: Convert with the scale first: cricket = 6 × 5 = 30, football = 4 × 5 = 20. Difference = 30 − 20 = 10 students. Answering '2' compares grid units and forgets each unit is worth 5; '30' merely restates cricket's total.

nodes.title: Integers: Multiplication, Division and Properties
nodes.description: Building on integer addition and subtraction, you will multiply and divide integers, master the sign rules (and why they work), and use properties like distributivity with negative numbers. These rules power all of algebra — every bracket you expand later depends on them.
learning_outcomes: Can multiply integers with any combination of signs and justify the sign of the product
Can divide integers and connect division to multiplication facts
Can apply commutativity, associativity and distributivity with negative numbers
Can solve multi-step problems mixing all four operations with integers

misconceptions.description: Believes negative × negative = negative ('two bad things stay bad').
misconceptions.remedy: Use the pattern approach: 3×(−6)=−18, 2×(−6)=−12, 1×(−6)=−6, 0×(−6)=0 … each step ADDS 6, so (−1)×(−6) must be +6. Also frame as reversing a reversal: the opposite of −6, taken 4 times.

misconceptions.description: Over-applies 'minus and minus make plus' to ADDITION: (−3) + (−5) = +8.
misconceptions.signal: Turns sums of two negatives positive, citing the multiplication rule.
misconceptions.remedy: Separate the contexts explicitly: the two-negatives rule belongs to multiplication/division only. Re-anchor addition in debts: owing ₹3 and owing ₹5 more is owing ₹8, never gaining.

misconceptions.description: Distributes a minus sign to only the first term: −(3 + 4) = −3 + 4.
misconceptions.signal: Bracket expansions where only the first term changes sign.
misconceptions.remedy: Read −(3+4) as (−1) × (3+4) and distribute the −1 to BOTH terms; check numerically: −(7) must equal −3 − 4 = −7, not +1.

misconceptions.description: Drops the sign in division (or applies sign rules inconsistently there): (−36) ÷ 4 = 9.
misconceptions.signal: Correct magnitudes but random or missing signs in quotients.
misconceptions.remedy: Convert every division to its multiplication check: (−36) ÷ 4 = q means q × 4 = −36, forcing q = −9. Same sign rules govern both operations.

real_world_hooks: Quiz scoring: +5 per correct answer, −2 per wrong answer — final scores
A water tank draining 3 litres per minute: level change after 8 minutes as (−3) × 8
Temperature dropping 2°C per hour through the night
Rewinding a video at 2× speed: reversing a reversal as negative × negative
teaching.video_search: multiplying dividing integers sign rules why negative times negative is positive class 7

questions.prompt: Compute: (−4) × (−6)

options.diagnosis: Added the magnitudes and kept a negative sign — treated × as +.
Added the magnitudes and applied the sign rule — right rule, wrong operation.

questions.explanation: Negative × negative = positive, so (−4) × (−6) = +24. One way to see it: (−4) × (−6) is the opposite of 4 × (−6) = −24, and the opposite of −24 is 24.

questions.prompt: Compute: (−36) ÷ 4

options.diagnosis: Subtracted 4 from 36 instead of dividing.
Multiplied instead of dividing.

questions.explanation: Check by multiplication: what times 4 gives −36? Since (−9) × 4 = −36, the quotient is −9. Unlike signs (negative ÷ positive) always give a negative result.

questions.prompt: In a quiz, each correct answer scores +5 and each wrong answer scores −2. Rahul got 6 answers correct and 7 wrong. What is his total score?

options.diagnosis: Assigned the negative to the correct answers instead of the wrong ones.
Counted only the correct answers; ignored the penalty entirely.

questions.explanation: Score = 6 × 5 + 7 × (−2) = 30 + (−14) = 16. Treating the penalty as +2 gives 30 + 14 = 44 — dropping the sign changes a penalty into a reward.

nodes.title: Fractions and Decimals: Multiplication and Division
nodes.description: You will multiply and divide fractions and decimals, understand 'of' as multiplication, and see why dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal. Along the way you will confront a big surprise: multiplying can make numbers smaller, and dividing can make them bigger.
learning_outcomes: Can multiply fractions (including mixed numbers) and interpret 'of' as multiplication
Can divide by a fraction using the reciprocal, and explain why the method works
Can multiply and divide decimals, placing the decimal point by counting decimal places
Can predict whether a product/quotient will be bigger or smaller than the starting number

misconceptions.description: When dividing fractions, inverts the wrong fraction (or both), e.g. 3/4 ÷ 1/2 computed as 4/3 × 1/2.
misconceptions.signal: Sometimes right, sometimes wrong on division — the flip lands on a random fraction.
misconceptions.remedy: Anchor the rule in meaning: a ÷ (1/2) asks 'how many halves fit in a?' — so the DIVISOR is what gets inverted (keep–change–flip, in that fixed order). Verify each answer by multiplying back.

misconceptions.description: Believes multiplication always makes numbers bigger and division always makes them smaller.
misconceptions.signal: Rejects 8 × 1/2 = 4 as impossible; picks the larger option by instinct on any multiplication.
misconceptions.remedy: Use 'of' language with areas: 1/2 of 8 is visibly 4. Build a prediction table: multiplying by more than 1 grows, by exactly 1 keeps, by less than 1 shrinks — then test with a calculator.

misconceptions.description: Multiplies fractions by cross-multiplying or by first finding common denominators (mixing up the addition procedure).
misconceptions.signal: Computes 2/3 × 4/5 as 10/12, or converts to fifteenths before multiplying.
misconceptions.remedy: Contrast the two procedures side by side on the same pair of fractions, with an area-model picture for multiplication (a 2/3-by-4/5 shaded rectangle has area 8/15) so 'tops times tops, bottoms times bottoms' has an image behind it.

misconceptions.description: Places the decimal point in a product by vertical alignment (as in addition): 0.3 × 0.2 = 0.6.
misconceptions.signal: Products of two decimals keep one decimal place; the student never counts places.
misconceptions.remedy: Route through fractions: 0.3 × 0.2 = 3/10 × 2/10 = 6/100 = 0.06. Then formalise: the product has as many decimal places as the two factors COMBINED. Estimation check: 0.3 × 0.2 must be less than 0.3.

real_world_hooks: Half of three-quarters of a pizza: 'of' as multiplication
How many 0.5 L bottles can you fill from a 3.75 L can?
Petrol at ₹104.50 per litre: cost of 2.4 litres
Scaling a recipe down to 2/3 for fewer guests
teaching.video_search: multiplying dividing fractions reciprocal decimal multiplication class 7

questions.prompt: Compute: 2/3 × 4/5

options.diagnosis: Added the fractions (10/15 + 12/15) instead of multiplying.
Added numerators and added denominators — neither multiplication nor correct addition.

questions.explanation: Multiply straight across: (2 × 4)/(3 × 5) = 8/15. Cross-multiplying (giving 10/12) belongs to comparing fractions, not multiplying them. Note 8/15 is smaller than both factors' larger one — taking 2/3 OF something shrinks it.

questions.prompt: Compute: 0.3 × 0.2

options.diagnosis: Added the decimals instead of multiplying.
Multiplied 3 × 2 and ignored both decimal points.

questions.explanation: 3 × 2 = 6, and the factors have 1 + 1 = 2 decimal places between them, so the product has two: 0.06. Fraction check: 3/10 × 2/10 = 6/100. Sense check: 0.3 of 0.2 must be SMALLER than 0.2 — so 0.6 cannot be right.

questions.prompt: A jug holds 3/4 litre of juice. How many 1/2-litre glasses can be completely or partly filled — that is, what is 3/4 ÷ 1/2?

options.diagnosis: Multiplied by 1/2 instead of dividing — forgot to invert the divisor.
Inverted BOTH fractions before multiplying.

questions.explanation: Keep–change–flip: 3/4 ÷ 1/2 = 3/4 × 2/1 = 6/4 = 3/2 = 1½. Meaning: one full half-litre glass fits in 3/4 L, with 1/4 L left — exactly half of another glass. Notice the quotient is BIGGER than 3/4: dividing by a number less than 1 enlarges.

nodes.title: Rational Numbers: Representation and Comparison
nodes.description: Rational numbers are all numbers expressible as p/q with integers p, q and q ≠ 0 — uniting integers, fractions and their negatives into one family. You will write rationals in standard form, place them on the number line, compare them, and find rationals between any two given ones.
learning_outcomes: Can write a rational number in standard form (positive denominator, lowest terms)
Can place positive and negative rationals on the number line
Can compare and order rational numbers, including negatives
Can find rational numbers between two given rational numbers

misconceptions.description: Orders negative rationals by magnitude: −3/4 > −1/2 'because 3/4 > 1/2'.
misconceptions.signal: Ranks negative fractions in the same order as their positive counterparts.
misconceptions.remedy: Plot both on a number line: −3/4 sits further LEFT than −1/2, so it is smaller. Rehearse the reflection principle: comparing negatives reverses the comparison of their positives.

misconceptions.description: Believes there are no (or only finitely many) rational numbers between two given rationals.
misconceptions.signal: Says 'nothing lies between 1/3 and 1/2' or counts a fixed handful.
misconceptions.remedy: Average the two numbers to exhibit one in between, then average again — the process never ends. Rewrite with bigger denominators (1/3 = 10/30, 1/2 = 15/30) to make room visibly.

misconceptions.description: Thinks integers (and terminating decimals) are not rational numbers.
misconceptions.signal: Sorts 5 or −3 outside the 'rational' circle in a classification task.
misconceptions.remedy: Write each as p/q: 5 = 5/1, −3 = −3/1, 0.7 = 7/10. Draw the nested-sets diagram: integers sit inside the rationals.

misconceptions.description: Treats −5/8, 5/−8 and −(5/8) as three different numbers, or misplaces the sign in standard form.
misconceptions.signal: Cannot decide whether 12/−18 is positive or negative; leaves negative denominators in answers.
misconceptions.remedy: Establish that one negative sign anywhere makes the whole number negative, and standard form parks the sign in the numerator; verify equivalence by dividing on a calculator.

real_world_hooks: Temperatures between −1°C and 0°C on a winter night in the hills
Profit/loss per share on the stock ticker: −2.5, +0.75
Sea level as 0: heights and depths as positive and negative rationals
Zooming into a digital measuring scale: always more marks between marks
teaching.video_search: rational numbers standard form number line comparison class 7

questions.prompt: Write 12/−18 in standard form.

options.diagnosis: Moved the sign correctly but only divided by 2; standard form needs lowest terms.
Inverted the fraction while simplifying.

questions.explanation: One negative sign makes the number negative: 12/−18 = −12/18. Divide top and bottom by HCF 6: −2/3. Standard form = negative sign (if any) on top, denominator positive, lowest terms.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the GREATEST: −1/2, −3/4, −7/8, −1?

options.diagnosis: Partial ordering: beat some options but still compared magnitudes the wrong way round.

questions.explanation: All four are negative, so the one CLOSEST to zero is greatest. On the number line from left to right: −1, −7/8, −3/4, −1/2. Hence −1/2 is greatest — for negatives, bigger magnitude means smaller number.

questions.prompt: Which rational number lies between 1/3 and 1/2?

options.text: There is no rational number between them

options.diagnosis: 2/6 equals 1/3 itself — equivalent fractions overlooked; 'between' must be strictly between.
Arithmetic slip while averaging: 7/12 is bigger than 1/2 = 6/12, so it lies outside the interval.

questions.explanation: Convert to twelfths: 1/3 = 4/12 and 1/2 = 6/12, so 5/12 sits strictly between. (It is exactly their average.) Between ANY two distinct rationals there are infinitely many more — just keep averaging.

nodes.title: Comparing Quantities: Percentage, Profit and Loss, Simple Interest
nodes.description: Percentages turn every comparison into 'per hundred', making unlike things comparable. You will convert between fractions, decimals and percents, compute percentage increase/decrease, profit and loss on cost price, and simple interest. These are the most-used school mathematics in adult life.
learning_outcomes: Can convert fluently between fractions, decimals and percentages
Can find a percentage of a quantity and express one quantity as a percentage of another
Can compute profit/loss and profit/loss percent on the cost price
Can compute simple interest with SI = P × R × T / 100 and find the amount

misconceptions.description: Compares or adds percentages of DIFFERENT bases as if they were plain numbers ('10% of my money plus 10% of yours = 20%').
misconceptions.signal: Claims a 50% score in one test and 50% in another 'add to 100%', or that 20% off a cheap item beats 10% off an expensive one automatically.
misconceptions.remedy: Force the base into every statement: '20% OF WHAT?' Compute rupee values side by side (20% of ₹100 = ₹20 vs 10% of ₹500 = ₹50) until percent-without-base sounds incomplete.

misconceptions.description: Computes profit percent on the selling price instead of the cost price.
misconceptions.remedy: Fix the reference: profit percent answers 'how much did the money INVESTED grow?' — the base is what you paid. Label CP explicitly as the base in every problem before computing.

misconceptions.description: Treats the percent number as a rupee/quantity answer (25% of 200 is '25'), or drops the /100 in formulas.
misconceptions.signal: Answers with the rate itself; simple-interest answers off by a factor of 100.
misconceptions.remedy: Translate percent to a fraction EVERY time before computing: 25% = 25/100 = 1/4, so 25% of 200 = 200/4 = 50. Keep units attached: percent is a rate, rupees are money.

misconceptions.description: Believes an x% increase followed by an x% decrease returns to the original value.
misconceptions.signal: Says a price raised 10% then cut 10% is unchanged.
misconceptions.remedy: Compute a concrete case: ₹100 → ₹110 → ₹99. Discuss why: the 10% cut acts on a BIGGER base than the 10% rise did. This previews successive-change problems in Class 8.

real_world_hooks: Sale season: '25% OFF' tags and comparing final UPI amounts across shops
A shopkeeper buys at wholesale (CP) and sells at retail (SP) — profit percent
Bank FD or post-office savings: simple interest on a deposit
Exam scores: 18/25 vs 68/100 — which is better?
teaching.video_search: percentage profit loss simple interest word problems class 7

questions.prompt: Find 25% of 200.

options.diagnosis: Divided 200 by 25 instead of taking 25 hundredths of it.
Subtracted 25 from 200 — treated the percent as a rupee amount to remove.

questions.explanation: 25% means 25/100 = 1/4. One quarter of 200 is 50. The rate '25' is not itself the answer — it must act on the base 200.

questions.prompt: A trader buys a bag for ₹400 (CP) and sells it for ₹500 (SP). What is the profit percent?

options.diagnosis: Reported the rupee profit (₹100) with a percent sign attached.
Computed SP as a percent of CP but forgot to subtract the original 100%.

questions.explanation: Profit = 500 − 400 = ₹100. Profit% = profit/CP × 100 = 100/400 × 100 = 25%. Dividing by SP gives 20% — but the base for profit percent is always the cost price, the money originally put in.

questions.prompt: Meera deposits ₹5,000 at 8% per annum simple interest. How much interest does she earn in 2 years?

options.diagnosis: Computed one year's interest; forgot to multiply by the time (2 years).
Reported the total amount (principal + interest) instead of the interest alone.

questions.explanation: SI = P × R × T / 100 = 5000 × 8 × 2 / 100 = ₹800. The amount she would hold at the end is 5000 + 800 = ₹5,800, but the question asks only for the interest earned.

nodes.title: Exponents and Powers: Laws and Standard Form
nodes.description: Exponents compress repeated multiplication: 10⁵ instead of 10×10×10×10×10. You will evaluate powers, use the laws of exponents (product, quotient, power of a power), and write large numbers in standard form. Exponents are the language of both astronomy and algebra.
learning_outcomes: Can evaluate powers with whole-number exponents, including powers of negative bases
Can apply a^m × a^n = a^(m+n), a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m−n) and (a^m)^n = a^(mn) with justification
Can use a⁰ = 1 (a ≠ 0) and explain it via the quotient pattern
Can express large numbers in standard form k × 10^n with 1 ≤ k < 10

misconceptions.description: Multiplies exponents when multiplying same-base powers: a^m × a^n = a^(mn).
misconceptions.signal: Writes 3⁴ × 3² = 3⁸.
misconceptions.remedy: Expand once fully: (3·3·3·3) × (3·3) is six 3s multiplied, so 3⁶. Derive each law from expansion at least once before allowing shortcut use.

misconceptions.description: Reads a power as base × exponent: 2³ = 6.
misconceptions.signal: Small powers systematically wrong: 2³=6, 5²=10.
misconceptions.remedy: Verbalise '2 used as a factor 3 times' and contrast the pair 2³ = 8 vs 2×3 = 6 explicitly; drill with cases where the two differ dramatically (10² vs 10×2).

misconceptions.description: Thinks a⁰ = 0 (or a⁰ = a).
misconceptions.signal: Writes 7⁰ = 0.
misconceptions.remedy: Walk down the ladder: 7³=343, 7²=49, 7¹=7 — each step divides by 7, so 7⁰ = 7/7 = 1. Also via the quotient law: 7² ÷ 7² = 7⁰ and any number divided by itself is 1.

misconceptions.description: In standard form, counts only the zeros (or the digits) to pick the power of 10.
misconceptions.signal: Writes 384,000 = 3.84 × 10³ 'because there are three zeros'.
misconceptions.remedy: Teach the decimal-shift method: count how many places the decimal point moves from after the leading digit to the end — for 384,000 it is 5 moves, so 10⁵. Verify by multiplying back.

real_world_hooks: Distance from Earth to Sun ≈ 1.5 × 10⁸ km — why scientists refuse to write all the zeros
Viral forwarding: one WhatsApp message forwarded to 3 people, each forwards to 3 more — powers of 3
Folding a paper in half repeatedly: thickness doubles as 2ⁿ
India's population written in standard form
teaching.video_search: laws of exponents standard form large numbers class 7

questions.prompt: What is 2³?

options.diagnosis: Swapped base and exponent: computed 3².
Added base and exponent.

questions.explanation: 2³ means 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 — the base 2 used as a factor three times. It is NOT 2 × 3; that confusion gives 6.

questions.prompt: Simplify: 3⁴ × 3²

options.diagnosis: Multiplied the bases as well; with the same base, the base stays put.

questions.explanation: 3⁴ × 3² = (3·3·3·3) × (3·3) = six 3s multiplied = 3⁶. When multiplying powers of the SAME base, add the exponents (4 + 2 = 6); the base does not change.

questions.prompt: Write 384,000 in standard form.

options.diagnosis: Equal in value, but standard form requires the first factor to be at least 1 and less than 10.
Off by one: counted all six digits instead of the five decimal shifts.

questions.explanation: Place the decimal after the leading digit: 3.84. The point moves 5 places to restore 384,000, so the power is 10⁵: 384,000 = 3.84 × 10⁵. Counting only the three zeros undercounts the shifts.

nodes.title: Simple Equations: Solving One-variable Linear Equations
nodes.description: An equation is a balance: whatever you do to one side you must do to the other. You will solve equations like 5x − 3 = 12 by systematic inverse operations (or transposition done with understanding), check solutions by substitution, and translate word problems into equations.
learning_outcomes: Can maintain balance: perform the same operation on both sides of an equation
Can solve one- and two-step linear equations in one variable, including with integer solutions
Can verify a solution by substituting it back into the original equation
Can set up and solve an equation from a word problem

misconceptions.description: Transposes terms without changing the operation/sign: from x + 7 = 15 gets x = 15 + 7.
misconceptions.signal: Moves numbers across '=' unchanged; answers consistently overshoot or undershoot.
misconceptions.remedy: Re-derive transposition from balance moves: subtract 7 from BOTH sides and watch the +7 'become' −7 on the other side. Ban blind rule-use until the student can narrate the both-sides version.

misconceptions.description: Applies an operation to only one side (or only one term) of the equation.
misconceptions.signal: From x/3 = 4 writes x = 4 (multiplied the left by 3 only), or halves a single term.
misconceptions.remedy: Use a physical or drawn pan balance: removing weight from one pan visibly tilts it. Insist on writing the operation on both sides on separate lines before simplifying.

misconceptions.description: Thinks '=' means 'the answer is', so the number on the right IS x, and an equation is an instruction to compute left-to-right.
misconceptions.signal: For x + 5 = 12 answers x = 12; resists equations written as 12 = x + 5.
misconceptions.remedy: Present equations in varied formats (12 = x + 5, x + 5 = 3 + 9) and use the balance metaphor: '=' states that two expressions weigh the same, it does not announce a result.

misconceptions.description: Does not check solutions; accepts any computed number even when substitution fails.
misconceptions.signal: Submits x = 9/5 for 5x − 3 = 12 without noticing 5(9/5) − 3 = 6 ≠ 12.
