misconceptions.remedy: Make substitution the mandatory last step with a written ✓/✗; celebrate catches — a failed check is information, pointing back to the exact wrong move.

real_world_hooks: A pan balance with hidden-mass bags: physically solving 2x + 1 = 7
Mobile recharge puzzle: after spending ₹37 you have ₹63 — what did you start with?
Auto fare: total ₹85 at ₹25 base plus ₹12/km — how far did you ride?
'Think of a number' magic tricks reversed step by step
teaching.video_search: solving simple linear equations balance method transposition class 7

questions.prompt: Solve: x + 7 = 15

options.diagnosis: Echoed the other visible number; no solving move was made.

questions.explanation: Subtract 7 from both sides: x + 7 − 7 = 15 − 7, so x = 8. Check: 8 + 7 = 15 ✓. Moving the 7 across without flipping to subtraction gives 22 — and 22 + 7 is 29, not 15, so the check catches it.

questions.prompt: Solve: 5x − 3 = 12

options.diagnosis: Multiplied by 5 in the last step instead of dividing — inverted the inverse operation.
Divided 15 by 3 (the wrong number) — coefficient and constant swapped roles.

questions.explanation: Add 3 to both sides: 5x = 15. Divide both sides by 5: x = 3. Check: 5(3) − 3 = 12 ✓. Transposing −3 without flipping gives 5x = 9, x = 1.8, and the check fails: 5(1.8) − 3 = 6 ≠ 12.

questions.prompt: The sum of three consecutive whole numbers is 63. What is the SMALLEST of them?

options.diagnosis: Solved 3x = 63 directly, forgetting the +1 and +2 — that gives the middle number, not the smallest.
Found the largest of the three numbers; misread which one was asked.
Stopped at 3x = 60 without dividing by 3.

questions.explanation: Let the numbers be x, x+1, x+2. Then 3x + 3 = 63, so 3x = 60 and x = 20. The numbers are 20, 21, 22 (sum 63 ✓); the smallest is 20. Note 21 is the middle number — the mean — not the smallest.

nodes.title: Algebraic Expressions: Terms, Like Terms, Evaluation
nodes.description: You will take expressions apart into terms, factors and coefficients, combine like terms, add and subtract whole expressions, and evaluate them for given values — including negative ones. Fluency here is what makes equation-solving and identities feel easy next year.
learning_outcomes: Can identify terms, factors, coefficients, and classify monomials/binomials/trinomials
Can identify like terms and combine them correctly
Can add and subtract algebraic expressions, distributing the minus sign over every term
Can evaluate expressions at given values, including negative values

misconceptions.description: Combines unlike terms: 2a + 4b = 6ab, or x + x² = x³.
misconceptions.signal: Any sum collapses to a single term; variables get glued together.
misconceptions.remedy: Use the fruit-crate test carefully re-worded numerically: substitute a = 2, b = 3 and compare 2a + 4b = 16 with 6ab = 36. Sort terms into like-term bins by their exact variable part before adding.

misconceptions.description: When subtracting an expression, applies the minus sign only to the first term: (4a+3b) − (2a−b) = 4a + 3b − 2a − b.
misconceptions.signal: Sign of the second and later terms of the subtracted bracket left unchanged.
misconceptions.remedy: Rewrite subtraction as adding (−1) × (bracket) and distribute the −1 to EVERY term, drawing arrows to each one. Check with numbers afterwards.

misconceptions.description: Mishandles squares of negative values: (−2)² computed as −4.
misconceptions.signal: Evaluation errors whenever the substituted value is negative; confuses (−2)² with −2².
misconceptions.remedy: Bracket discipline: substitute with brackets ALWAYS — (−2)² = (−2)(−2) = 4. Contrast (−2)² and −(2²) explicitly as different expressions.

misconceptions.description: Thinks a lone variable has coefficient 0 (or that −x has coefficient 1).
misconceptions.signal: Says the coefficient of x in x + 5 is 0 'because nothing is written'.
misconceptions.remedy: Rewrite invisibly-coefficient terms explicitly: x = 1·x, −x = (−1)·x, then combine like terms with the coefficients visible.

real_world_hooks: Canteen orders: 3 samosas + 2 teas can't merge into '5 samosa-teas' — like terms only
Perimeter expressions for garden plots with unknown sides
Total marks formula across tests with different weightings
Simplifying a shopping bill written with x kg onions and y kg tomatoes
teaching.video_search: algebraic expressions like terms adding subtracting evaluating class 7

questions.prompt: Simplify: 5x + 3x

options.diagnosis: Multiplied the variables while adding coefficients; adding like terms never changes the power.
Multiplied the coefficients instead of adding them.
Dropped the variable; 5x + 3x means 5 x's plus 3 x's, which is 8 x's.

questions.explanation: 5x and 3x are like terms (same variable part x), so add the coefficients: (5 + 3)x = 8x. Think '5 mangoes + 3 mangoes = 8 mangoes' — the unit x stays as it is.

questions.prompt: Simplify: (4a + 3b) − (2a − b)

options.diagnosis: Subtracted the first expression from the second — order of subtraction reversed.

questions.explanation: Distribute the minus over BOTH terms of the second bracket: 4a + 3b − 2a + b. Combine like terms: (4a − 2a) + (3b + b) = 2a + 4b. Forgetting to flip −b to +b gives 2a + 2b — the classic slip.

questions.prompt: Evaluate 3x² + 2x when x = −2.

options.diagnosis: Dropped the sign in 2x: computed 12 + 4 instead of 12 − 4.

questions.explanation: Substitute with brackets: 3(−2)² + 2(−2) = 3(4) + (−4) = 12 − 4 = 8. The trap is (−2)²: squaring a negative gives POSITIVE 4. Writing −2² without brackets is how the −16 and −8 answers arise.

nodes.title: Lines and Angles: Angle Pairs, Parallel Lines and Transversals
nodes.description: You will work with complementary, supplementary, adjacent and vertically opposite angles, then study what happens when a transversal cuts parallel lines: corresponding and alternate angles are equal, and co-interior angles add to 180°. These angle facts are the raw material of all later geometric proof.
learning_outcomes: Can find complements (to 90°) and supplements (to 180°) of given angles
Can identify and use vertically opposite angles and linear pairs
Can name corresponding, alternate and co-interior angle pairs at a transversal
Can compute unknown angles when a transversal cuts parallel lines, justifying each step

misconceptions.description: Swaps complementary (90°) and supplementary (180°).
misconceptions.signal: Gives 145° as the 'complement' of 35°.
misconceptions.remedy: Attach memory anchors: C comes before S just as 90 comes before 180; 'Corner' (90°) vs 'Straight' (180°). Then practise sorted pairs until the sorting is automatic.

misconceptions.description: Thinks vertically opposite angles are supplementary rather than equal (or must 'look' equal to be equal).
misconceptions.signal: Given one angle of an X as 70°, computes the opposite one as 110°.
misconceptions.remedy: Trace two crossing sticks and rotate one copy 180° about the crossing point — the opposite angles land exactly on each other. Distinguish them from the ADJACENT angles, which do form the 180° pairs.

misconceptions.description: Believes co-interior (allied) angles between parallel lines are equal, instead of supplementary.
misconceptions.signal: Marks both co-interior angles 65°.
misconceptions.remedy: Sort the three pairings physically with tracing paper: pairs that map onto each other by sliding (corresponding) or half-turn (alternate) are equal; the co-interior pair together forms a straight-line 'C/U shape' summing to 180°.

misconceptions.description: Applies parallel-line angle rules to ANY transversal diagram, even when the lines are not parallel.
misconceptions.signal: Claims alternate angles are equal in a triangle diagram with clearly non-parallel lines.
misconceptions.remedy: Show a counterexample with visibly non-parallel lines and measured angles. Institute the habit: before using any rule, state WHICH two lines are parallel and how you know.

real_world_hooks: Railway tracks (parallel lines) crossed by a road — the transversal angles
Scissors opening: vertically opposite angles staying equal
Window grills and ladder rungs: corresponding angles
Zebra crossings striping a road at an angle
teaching.video_search: parallel lines transversal corresponding alternate co-interior angles class 7

questions.prompt: What is the complement of 35°?

options.diagnosis: Thought 'complement' means an equal partner angle.
Arithmetic slip: subtracted from 100 instead of 90.

questions.explanation: Complementary angles sum to 90°: 90 − 35 = 55°. Supplementary angles sum to 180° — that is where 145° comes from, answering a different question.

questions.prompt: Two lines intersect. One of the angles formed is 70°. What is the angle VERTICALLY OPPOSITE to it?

options.diagnosis: Doubled the angle — no angle relationship at a crossing does this.

questions.explanation: Vertically opposite angles are always EQUAL, so it is 70°. The angles ADJACENT to the 70° angle are its supplements, 110° each — the 110° answer mixes up the two relationships.

questions.prompt: A transversal cuts two parallel lines. One of a pair of co-interior angles measures 65°. What is the other?

options.diagnosis: Subtracted from 90° — used the complement instead of the supplement.
Doubled 65° — perhaps confusing 'co-interior' with 'twice interior'.

questions.explanation: Co-interior angles between parallel lines are supplementary: 180 − 65 = 115°. It is the corresponding and alternate pairs that are EQUAL — co-interior angles instead complete a straight 'C' shape of 180°.

nodes.title: The Triangle and Its Properties: Angle Sum, Exterior Angle, Pythagoras Intro
nodes.description: Every triangle hides three strong laws: its angles sum to 180°, an exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles, and any two sides together exceed the third. For right triangles you will meet the Pythagoras property relating the squares on the sides.
learning_outcomes: Can use the angle-sum property (180°) to find unknown angles
Can apply the exterior-angle property: exterior = sum of the two remote interior angles
Can test whether three lengths can form a triangle (triangle inequality)
Can use the Pythagoras property to check for right angles and find a missing side in simple cases

misconceptions.description: Uses 360° as the angle sum of a triangle (confusing it with quadrilaterals or full turns).
misconceptions.signal: Third-angle answers that are about 180° too big.
misconceptions.remedy: Tear the three corners off a paper triangle and line them up along a ruler edge — they form a straight 180°, not a full turn. Repeat with differently shaped triangles.

misconceptions.description: Takes the exterior angle to be (or to pair with) the ADJACENT interior angle rather than the sum of the two remote ones.
misconceptions.signal: Computes the exterior angle as 180° minus the wrong angle, or equal to its neighbour.
misconceptions.remedy: Colour-code: shade the two REMOTE interior angles, then show both derivations agree — exterior = 180 − adjacent = (sum of all three) − adjacent = sum of the remote two.

misconceptions.description: Applies the Pythagoras property to non-right triangles (any triangle with a longest side).
misconceptions.signal: Writes a² + b² = c² for a triangle never stated to be right-angled.
misconceptions.remedy: Test the relation on an obtuse and an acute triangle with measured sides — it fails both ways. Establish the checklist: identify the right angle FIRST, then the hypotenuse opposite it.

misconceptions.description: Believes any three lengths can form a triangle.
misconceptions.signal: Happily 'constructs' a 3-4-8 triangle in numbers, never noticing it cannot close.
misconceptions.remedy: Hand over sticks (or straws) of lengths 3, 4 and 8 and let the student physically fail to close the triangle; formulate the rule from the experience: each side must be less than the sum of the other two.

real_world_hooks: A ladder leaning on a wall: the right triangle and Pythagoras
Triangular truss bridges and roof frames — why triangles are rigid
Shortcut across a rectangular park: diagonal vs walking two sides (triangle inequality)
Ramp design: rise, run and slope length
teaching.video_search: triangle angle sum exterior angle property triangle inequality pythagoras class 7

questions.prompt: Two angles of a triangle are 60° and 70°. What is the third angle?

options.diagnosis: Added the two given angles but never subtracted from 180°.
Averaged the two given angles — no such property exists.

questions.explanation: Angles of a triangle sum to 180°: third angle = 180 − (60 + 70) = 50°. Using 360° as the sum gives the impossible 230° — 360° belongs to quadrilaterals and full turns.

questions.prompt: In a triangle, the two interior angles remote from an exterior angle measure 40° and 60°. What is the exterior angle?

options.diagnosis: Added the adjacent interior angle into the sum as well.
Subtracted the remote angles instead of adding them.

questions.explanation: Exterior angle = sum of the two remote interior angles = 40 + 60 = 100°. Check via the straight line: the adjacent interior angle is 180 − 100 = 80° and indeed 80 + 40 + 60 = 180° ✓.

questions.prompt: Can the lengths 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm form a triangle?

options.text: No — 3 + 4 = 7 < 8, so the two short sides cannot reach across the longest one
Yes — any three lengths can form a triangle
No — because 3² + 4² ≠ 8², it is not right-angled
Yes — because the total 3 + 4 + 8 = 15 is greater than 8
options.diagnosis: Garbled inequality: the test compares the SUM OF TWO sides with the third, not the total with one side.

questions.explanation: Triangle inequality: EACH side must be shorter than the sum of the other two. Here 3 + 4 = 7 < 8, so the sides cannot close up. Pythagoras is irrelevant — failing a² + b² = c² only rules out a RIGHT triangle, not all triangles.

nodes.title: Congruence of Triangles: SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS
nodes.description: Two figures are congruent when one fits exactly on the other. For triangles you don't need to check all six parts: the criteria SSS, SAS, ASA and RHS each guarantee congruence from just three well-chosen parts. Congruence is your first taste of deductive proof.
learning_outcomes: Can state what congruence means and write correspondences (ΔABC ≅ ΔPQR) in the right order
Can select and apply the appropriate criterion: SSS, SAS, ASA or RHS
Can explain why AAA and SSA are NOT valid congruence criteria
Can extract equal corresponding parts (CPCT) from a stated congruence

misconceptions.description: Believes AAA (three equal angles) proves triangles congruent.
misconceptions.signal: Cites 'AAA' as a criterion; concludes congruence from angles alone.
misconceptions.remedy: Show two nested equilateral triangles of different sizes: same three angles, obviously different triangles. Angles fix the SHAPE but not the SIZE — that needs at least one side.

misconceptions.description: Uses SSA (two sides and a non-included angle) as a valid criterion.
misconceptions.signal: Applies 'SAS' with an angle that is not between the two sides.
misconceptions.remedy: Construct the ambiguous case: with two fixed sides and a non-included angle, the compass arc crosses the ray in TWO places, giving two different triangles. Emphasise 'included' by physically pointing at the angle BETWEEN the sides.

misconceptions.description: Judges congruence by appearance or area: 'they look the same size, so they are congruent'.
misconceptions.signal: Declares congruence without matching any parts; accepts a mirror-image or same-area shape as 'the same'.
misconceptions.remedy: Insist on superposition evidence (tracing paper) or a named criterion. Show two different rectangles with the same area (2×6, 3×4) to split 'equal area' from 'congruent'.

misconceptions.description: Ignores correspondence order in the congruence statement: reads ΔABC ≅ ΔPQR as 'any vertex matches any vertex'.
misconceptions.signal: Extracts wrong equal pairs (e.g. ∠A = ∠R) from a written congruence.
misconceptions.remedy: Highlight matching positions in the two names with the same colour (1st↔1st, 2nd↔2nd, 3rd↔3rd) and practise reading off all six equal parts from the statement alone.

real_world_hooks: Stamping and die-cutting: every biscuit from the same cutter is congruent
Machine parts and spare components must be congruent to fit
Trusses on a bridge built from identical triangles
Why your two phone-case copies fit the same phone
teaching.video_search: congruence of triangles SSS SAS ASA RHS criteria class 7

questions.prompt: Two triangles have two pairs of equal sides and the angles INCLUDED between those sides equal. Which congruence criterion applies?

options.diagnosis: Mixed up which parts are given: ASA needs two angles with the included side.
SSS needs all three sides; here only two sides are known.

questions.explanation: Side–Angle–Side: two sides and the angle BETWEEN them determine the triangle completely. The order of letters encodes the arrangement — the angle must sit between the two given sides.

questions.prompt: Two triangles have all three pairs of corresponding angles equal. Must they be congruent?

options.text: Not necessarily — one may be an enlargement of the other
Yes, provided they also look the same size
No — equal angles tell us nothing at all about the triangles
options.diagnosis: Over-correction: equal angles DO fix the shape (similarity); they just don't fix the size.

questions.explanation: Equal angles make triangles SIMILAR (same shape), not necessarily congruent (same shape AND size). A small and a large equilateral triangle share all angles yet aren't congruent. That is exactly why AAA is not a congruence criterion.

questions.prompt: Given ΔABC ≅ ΔPQR, which angle must be equal to ∠B?

options.text: Cannot be determined from the statement
options.diagnosis: The congruence statement's letter order IS the correspondence — it fully determines every matching part.

questions.explanation: In ΔABC ≅ ΔPQR the vertices correspond by position: A↔P, B↔Q, C↔R. So ∠B = ∠Q. Reading off corresponding parts this way is what 'corresponding parts of congruent triangles' (CPCT) means.

nodes.title: Symmetry: Line and Rotational
nodes.description: Beyond mirror lines, shapes can also match themselves under turning: a shape has rotational symmetry of order n if it looks unchanged n times during a full 360° turn. You will find orders and angles of rotation, and discover that line symmetry and rotational symmetry are independent properties.
learning_outcomes: Can find the order of rotational symmetry of a figure and its angle of rotation (360°/order)
Can locate the centre of rotation of a symmetric figure
Can give examples of shapes with line symmetry only, rotational only, both, and neither
Can explain why every figure trivially matches itself after a full 360° turn (order at least 1)

misconceptions.description: Miscounts the order — e.g. excludes the final position (square = order 3) or includes extra positions.
misconceptions.signal: Consistent off-by-one answers for order of rotational symmetry.
misconceptions.remedy: Physically rotate a cut-out with a mark on one corner, tallying every position (90°, 180°, 270°, 360°) where the outline matches. Define order as the number of matches in one FULL turn, including the return home.

misconceptions.description: Assumes line symmetry and rotational symmetry always come together.
misconceptions.signal: Concludes a parallelogram has mirror lines because it has half-turn symmetry, or that shapes like S/Z have no symmetry at all.
misconceptions.remedy: Build a 2×2 sorting grid (line? / rotational?) and place counterexamples in every cell: isosceles trapezium (line only), parallelogram and letter S (rotation only), square (both), scalene triangle (neither).

misconceptions.description: Confuses the ORDER with the ANGLE of rotation ('a square has symmetry of order 90').
misconceptions.signal: Answers in degrees when order is asked, or vice versa.
misconceptions.remedy: Drill the relationship angle = 360° ÷ order with a table (order 2 ↔ 180°, order 3 ↔ 120°, order 4 ↔ 90°), and always ask for both numbers together until they separate cleanly.

misconceptions.description: Believes a parallelogram's diagonals are lines of symmetry.
misconceptions.signal: Draws mirror lines along the diagonals of a generic parallelogram.
misconceptions.remedy: Fold a paper parallelogram along a diagonal — the halves do not coincide (they are congruent but flipped the wrong way). Contrast with the rhombus, where the diagonal fold DOES work.

real_world_hooks: Fan blades and wind turbines: rotational symmetry of order 3
Car wheel rims and alloy designs: what order do you see?
The Ashoka Chakra with 24 spokes
Playing cards that look the same upside down — half-turn symmetry
teaching.video_search: rotational symmetry order angle of rotation examples class 7

questions.prompt: What is the order of rotational symmetry of a square?

options.diagnosis: Added the 4 mirror lines to the 4 rotations — mixing the two kinds of symmetry.

questions.explanation: Rotating a square about its centre, it matches its outline at 90°, 180°, 270° and 360° — four positions in a full turn, so order 4. The angle of rotation is 90°; the order is the COUNT, not the angle.

questions.prompt: Which is true of a parallelogram that is neither a rectangle nor a rhombus?

options.text: It has NO line of symmetry but rotational symmetry of order 2
Its two diagonals are lines of symmetry
It has one vertical line of symmetry and no rotational symmetry
options.diagnosis: Guessing from the rectangle; a generic parallelogram fails every fold test.

options.text: It has 2 lines of symmetry because it has rotational symmetry of order 2

questions.explanation: A half-turn (180°) about the intersection of the diagonals maps a parallelogram onto itself — order 2. Yet no fold works: diagonal folds leave flipped, non-matching halves. It is the standard example that rotational symmetry can exist WITHOUT line symmetry.

questions.prompt: A figure has rotational symmetry of order 3. What is its (smallest) angle of rotation?

options.diagnosis: Used 360 ÷ 6 — perhaps doubled the order or halved the correct angle.
Defaulted to the half-turn; 180° is the angle for order 2.

questions.explanation: Angle of rotation = 360° ÷ order = 360 ÷ 3 = 120°. An equilateral triangle is the classic example: it matches itself every 120° of turn.

nodes.title: Visualising Solid Shapes: Nets, Sketches, Cross-sections
nodes.description: Solids live in 3D but we draw them in 2D. You will match solids with their nets, draw oblique and isometric sketches, imagine cross-sections made by cuts, and read views (top, front, side) and shadows. Strong 3D visualisation pays off in geometry, science diagrams and engineering drawing.
learning_outcomes: Can count and name faces, edges and vertices of common solids
Can decide whether a given net folds into a given solid (cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone)
Can describe the cross-section produced by a horizontal or vertical cut of a solid
Can interpret and draw top, front and side views of simple solid arrangements

misconceptions.description: Thinks ANY arrangement of 6 squares folds into a cube.
misconceptions.signal: Accepts a 2×3 block of squares, or a straight strip of 6, as a cube net.
misconceptions.remedy: Print several 6-square arrangements and actually fold them: some overlap faces and leave gaps. Develop checking strategies (no 2×2 block; at most 4 squares in a row) from the failures.

misconceptions.description: Believes every cross-section of a solid has the same shape as its base (e.g. all cuts of a cylinder are circles).
misconceptions.signal: Answers 'circle' for any cut of a cylinder, 'triangle' for any cut of a cone, regardless of direction.
misconceptions.remedy: Cut actual objects (cucumber, clay cylinder) horizontally AND vertically and trace the exposed faces: circle one way, rectangle the other. Make direction-of-cut a required part of every answer.

misconceptions.description: Reasons from the 2D drawing instead of the solid: counts only the visible faces or edges in a sketch.
misconceptions.signal: Says a cube has 3 faces 'because the picture shows 3'.
misconceptions.remedy: Keep a real cube in hand while reading sketches: rotate it to reveal hidden faces and mark dashed hidden edges on the drawing. Count on the object, then re-count on the sketch.

misconceptions.description: Mixes up faces, edges and vertices as interchangeable 'parts'.
misconceptions.signal: Reports 8 faces or 6 vertices for a cube; swaps the counts.
misconceptions.remedy: Attach each word to a gesture on a real solid: palm flat on a FACE, finger sliding along an EDGE, fingertip on a VERTEX (corner point). Tabulate F, E, V for several solids.

real_world_hooks: Unfolding a toothpaste carton or sweet box into its net
Cutting vegetables: cross-sections of a cucumber, onion rings
Dice: opposite faces of a die always total 7
Google Maps 2D view vs street view of the same building
teaching.video_search: nets of solids cross sections views of 3d shapes class 7

questions.prompt: How many faces does a cuboid have?
questions.explanation: A cuboid (like a matchbox) has 6 flat faces: top and bottom, front and back, left and right. A sketch shows only 3 at a time — the other 3 are hidden. It has 8 vertices and 12 edges, which is where those wrong counts come from.

questions.prompt: A cylinder is cut straight down, VERTICALLY through its centre. What is the shape of the cut face?

options.diagnosis: That comes from a SLANTED cut, not a vertical one.
Confusing the cylinder with a cone, whose vertical cut gives a triangle.

questions.explanation: A vertical cut through a cylinder exposes a rectangle — width equal to the diameter, height equal to the cylinder's height. Only HORIZONTAL cuts give circles; the cross-section's shape depends on the direction of the cut.

questions.prompt: On a standard die, opposite faces add up to 7. If 2 is on top, which number is on the bottom face?

options.diagnosis: Reported the sum itself instead of the missing partner.
Assumed the largest number sits opposite; the rule is about the SUM being 7.
Picked an adjacent (side) face rather than the opposite one — visualising the wrong face.

questions.explanation: Opposite faces sum to 7, so the face opposite 2 shows 7 − 2 = 5. The pairs on a standard die are 1–6, 2–5 and 3–4. Being able to 'see' the hidden bottom face from the visible top is exactly the visualisation skill this chapter builds.

nodes.title: Practical Geometry: Parallel Lines and Triangle Constructions
nodes.description: With ruler and compass you will construct a line parallel to a given line through a point, and triangles from given data: three sides (SSS), two sides and the included angle (SAS), two angles and a side (ASA), and right triangles (RHS). Each construction succeeds exactly when the corresponding congruence criterion holds — construction and congruence are two sides of the same coin.
learning_outcomes: Can construct a line parallel to a given line through an external point using equal alternate/corresponding angles
Can construct triangles from SSS, SAS, ASA and RHS data
Can recognise data sets that give no triangle (violating the triangle inequality) or more than one triangle
Can connect each construction to the congruence criterion that guarantees uniqueness

misconceptions.description: Believes any angle position works with two sides — uses a non-included angle as if it were SAS.
misconceptions.signal: Places the given angle at the wrong vertex and is surprised the triangle comes out different from a classmate's.
misconceptions.remedy: Have two students construct from the same SSA data and compare: two genuinely different triangles appear (the ambiguous case). Then re-construct with the INCLUDED angle and see uniqueness return.

misconceptions.description: Assumes any three measurements always produce a triangle.
misconceptions.signal: Given sides 4, 5, 10 keeps re-drawing arcs harder, blaming the compass when they never intersect.
misconceptions.remedy: Let the failure happen, then diagnose it: arcs of radii 4 and 5 from the ends of a 10-unit base can never meet since 4 + 5 < 10. Check the triangle inequality BEFORE constructing, every time.

misconceptions.description: 'Parallel' is judged by eye: slides the ruler and draws a line that merely looks parallel.
misconceptions.signal: Freehand or slid-ruler parallels; cannot say what property makes the lines parallel.
misconceptions.remedy: Tie the construction to angle facts: copying the transversal's angle at the new point forces equal corresponding (or alternate) angles, which is exactly the CONDITION for parallelism. Verify by measuring perpendicular distances at two places.

misconceptions.description: Treats construction steps as arbitrary ritual — cannot say why an arc or line is drawn, so errors go unnoticed.
misconceptions.signal: Reproduces sequences by rote, gets stuck when data is given in a different order.
misconceptions.remedy: After each construction, require a one-line justification per step ('this arc marks all points 5 cm from B'). Rebuild the same triangle starting from a different given part.

real_world_hooks: Drawing parallel lines for ruled pages, roads and railway plans
A carpenter making a triangular bracket exactly to specification
Why survey markers use triangles: three measurements pin a shape
Tailoring: cutting identical triangular panels from measurements
teaching.video_search: construct triangle SSS SAS ASA RHS parallel line through point compass class 7

questions.prompt: Which set of data lets you construct a UNIQUE triangle?

options.text: Two sides and the angle INCLUDED between them

options.diagnosis: Three angles fix the shape but not the size — infinitely many similar triangles fit.

options.text: Two sides and any one angle, wherever it is

questions.explanation: SAS data determines exactly one triangle — this is the SAS congruence criterion at work. Angles alone leave the size free; a non-included angle can give two different triangles; and three lengths only work when each is less than the sum of the other two.

questions.prompt: To construct a line through point P parallel to line l with ruler and compass, the standard method is to:

options.text: Draw a transversal through P meeting l, then copy the angle it makes with l at P (equal corresponding/alternate angles)
Slide a set-square along until the line through P looks parallel
Draw any line through P that does not touch l on the page
options.diagnosis: Lines extend beyond the page; not meeting in the drawing is not the same as never meeting.

options.text: Join P to any point of l and extend the segment
options.diagnosis: That line CROSSES l at the chosen point — the opposite of parallel.

questions.explanation: Equal corresponding (or alternate) angles with a transversal is precisely the condition that makes two lines parallel. Copying the angle at P with compass arcs builds that condition in exactly — no eyeballing required.

questions.prompt: You try to construct a triangle with sides 4 cm, 5 cm and 10 cm. What happens?

options.text: It is impossible — the arcs of radius 4 and 5 never intersect, since 4 + 5 < 10
It works — any three lengths give a triangle
It works, but only if you draw the 10 cm side first
It is impossible because a triangle's sides must all be different by at most 2 cm
options.diagnosis: Invented rule; the real test is the triangle inequality, not a fixed gap.

questions.explanation: From the ends of the 10 cm base, arcs of radii 4 cm and 5 cm reach at most 4 + 5 = 9 cm of combined stretch — they can never meet. The triangle inequality (each side < sum of the other two) fails, so NO order of steps can succeed.

nodes.title: Perimeter and Area: Triangles, Parallelograms, Circles
nodes.description: You will extend area from rectangles to parallelograms (base × height) and triangles (half of that), and meet the circle's two famous formulas: circumference 2πr and area πr². Choosing the RIGHT base–height pair, and the right formula, is the heart of this chapter.
learning_outcomes: Can compute areas of parallelograms and triangles using base and the PERPENDICULAR height
Can compute circumference and area of circles, using π ≈ 22/7 or 3.14
Can solve problems with paths, borders and combined figures
Can convert between units of area (cm², m²) where needed

misconceptions.description: Still conflates perimeter and area, choosing the wrong measure for the context.
misconceptions.signal: Computes 2(l+b) when asked how much surface to paint, or l×b for fencing.
misconceptions.remedy: Re-anchor with actions (walk the boundary vs cover the surface) and sort a mixed set of word problems into P-questions and A-questions BEFORE solving any.

misconceptions.description: Forgets the ½ in the triangle formula (or uses the slant side as the height).
misconceptions.signal: Triangle areas exactly double the correct value; uses a non-perpendicular side as 'height'.
misconceptions.remedy: Cut a paper parallelogram along a diagonal: two identical triangles, so each is HALF the parallelogram. For height, drop a set-square perpendicular from the apex — height must meet the base at 90°.

misconceptions.description: Swaps the circle formulas: uses πr² for circumference and 2πr for area.
misconceptions.signal: Circumference answers with square units of magnitude r²; area answers linear in r.
misconceptions.remedy: Use dimension sense: circumference is a LENGTH (one r ⇒ 2πr), area is a SURFACE (r × r ⇒ πr²). Wrap a string round a tin (≈ 3 diameters plus a bit) to make 2πr concrete.

misconceptions.description: Treats any given pair of numbers as base and height, even when one is a slant length.
misconceptions.signal: In a parallelogram with side 6, base 8, height 5, computes area 6 × 8.
misconceptions.remedy: Mark the right-angle symbol in every figure first; the height is the measurement carrying that symbol. Practise on figures deliberately labelled with a distracting slant side.

real_world_hooks: Cricket ground: boundary rope length (circumference) vs outfield grass (area)
Samosa maths: triangular area from a folded square
Cycle wheel: how far does one full rotation take you? (2πr)
Paving a path around a rectangular park
teaching.video_search: area triangle parallelogram circle circumference formula class 7

questions.prompt: Find the area of a triangle with base 10 cm and height 6 cm.

options.diagnosis: Added base and height instead of multiplying.
Halved only the base and then added the height — formula fragments recombined wrongly.

questions.explanation: Area = ½ × base × height = ½ × 10 × 6 = 30 cm². Without the ½ you get the area of the parallelogram (60) that two copies of this triangle would tile.

questions.prompt: A parallelogram has base 8 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm. Its area is:

options.diagnosis: Halved like a triangle; the parallelogram formula has no ½.
Added the two measurements instead of multiplying.

questions.explanation: Area of a parallelogram = base × perpendicular height = 8 × 5 = 40 cm². (Slicing off the slanted end and sliding it across turns it into an 8 × 5 rectangle.) 26 cm would be a perimeter-style calculation — the wrong measure.

questions.prompt: Taking π = 22/7, find the CIRCUMFERENCE of a circle of radius 7 cm.

options.diagnosis: Computed πr, forgetting the factor 2 — that is only half the boundary.
Computed r² and stopped — a fragment of the area formula.

questions.explanation: Circumference = 2πr = 2 × (22/7) × 7 = 44 cm. The value 154 is the AREA, πr² = (22/7) × 49 — right numbers, wrong formula. Dimension check: circumference is a length, so the formula uses r once, not r².

nodes.title: Data Handling: Mean, Median, Mode, Range and Chance
nodes.description: One number can represent a whole data set: the mean (fair share), median (middle of the sorted list) and mode (most frequent value) — each useful in different situations, with range measuring spread. You will also take your first formal steps into probability as a number between 0 and 1.
learning_outcomes: Can compute the mean and explain it as equal sharing / balance point
Can find the median (after sorting!) and the mode of a data set
Can choose which average best represents a data set and critique a poor choice
Can assign simple probabilities as favourable outcomes over total equally likely outcomes

misconceptions.description: Believes the mean must be one of the data values (or must be a whole number).
misconceptions.signal: Rejects 6 as the mean of 2, 3, 7, 12 'because 6 isn't in the list', or rounds means to force them into the data.
misconceptions.remedy: Use the levelling model: stack unifix cubes in towers of 2, 3, 7, 12 and move cubes until all towers are equal — height 6 appears even though no tower started at 6.

misconceptions.description: Finds the median of the list AS GIVEN, without sorting first.
misconceptions.signal: Picks the physically middle number of the unsorted list.
misconceptions.remedy: Make sorting a non-negotiable first step: have students physically line up in height order before finding the middle person. Contrast median-of-unsorted vs median-of-sorted on the same data.

misconceptions.description: Confuses mode with the largest value (or mean with the middle).
misconceptions.signal: Reports the maximum as the mode; mixes the three M-words freely.
misconceptions.remedy: Anchor each word: MOde = MOst often, meDIAN = midDIAN (middle of the road), mean = share out evenly. Compute all three for one small data set and label them on a dot plot.

misconceptions.description: Treats all outcomes as 50-50 because 'it either happens or it doesn't'.
misconceptions.signal: Says the chance of drawing a red ball from 3 red and 7 blue is 1/2.
misconceptions.remedy: Run the experiment: 20 draws from a 3-red/7-blue bag almost never gives half red. Rebuild probability as favourable/total with all outcomes listed and checked for equal likelihood.

real_world_hooks: Batting average vs 'most common score' — why Kohli's average isn't a score he often makes
Median house rent in your area vs the mean skewed by one luxury flat
Class test: mean, median and mode of everyone's marks
Chance of rain, coin tosses at a cricket match
teaching.video_search: mean median mode range probability introduction class 7

questions.prompt: Find the mean of 2, 3, 7 and 12.

options.diagnosis: Found the total but forgot to divide by the number of values.
Found the median ((3+7)/2) — a valid average, but not the mean asked for.

questions.explanation: Mean = (2 + 3 + 7 + 12) ÷ 4 = 24 ÷ 4 = 6. Notice 6 is not one of the data values — that is perfectly fine; the mean is the equal-share value, not necessarily a member of the list.

questions.prompt: Find the median of 7, 2, 9, 4, 6.

options.diagnosis: Computed the mean (28 ÷ 5) instead of the median.
Sorted correctly but took the wrong position — off by one from the middle.

questions.explanation: Sort first: 2, 4, 6, 7, 9. With five values, the middle (third) one is 6. Taking the middle of the UNSORTED list gives 9 — sorting is what makes the median meaningful.

questions.prompt: A bag contains 3 red and 7 blue balls. One ball is drawn without looking. What is the probability that it is red?

options.diagnosis: Compared red with blue (part-to-part odds) instead of red with ALL balls.
Found the probability of blue — the complement of what was asked.

questions.explanation: There are 10 equally likely balls, of which 3 are favourable: P(red) = 3/10. 'Red or not red' are two DESCRIPTIONS, not two equally likely outcomes — so 1/2 is wrong; and 3/7 compares the wrong pair (red against blue, rather than red against the total).

nodes.title: Rational Numbers: Properties and Density
nodes.description: You will study rational numbers as a system: closure, commutativity and associativity, the roles of 0 and 1, negatives (additive inverses) and reciprocals (multiplicative inverses), and distributivity as a computation shortcut. The headline property is density — between any two rationals lie infinitely many more.
learning_outcomes: Can state and use the properties of operations on rational numbers, with counterexamples for subtraction/division
Can find additive and multiplicative inverses and keep the two ideas apart
Can use distributivity to simplify computations like a×b + a×c
Can find (infinitely many) rational numbers between two given rationals

misconceptions.description: Thinks only finitely many (or no) rationals lie between two given rationals.
misconceptions.signal: Counts 'the numbers between 1/4 and 1/2' as a short finite list, usually via decimals to two places.
misconceptions.remedy: Iterate the midpoint construction live: between any two, their average; between THAT pair, another average — the supply never ends. Zooming on a number-line app makes the endlessness visceral.

misconceptions.description: Confuses additive inverse (opposite) with multiplicative inverse (reciprocal).
misconceptions.signal: Answers 3/2 when asked for the additive inverse of −2/3... or −(2/3) for the reciprocal; mixes sign-flip with flip-over.
misconceptions.remedy: Tie each inverse to its identity: opposite makes the SUM zero (x + ? = 0); reciprocal makes the PRODUCT one (x × ? = 1). Always write the defining equation before answering.

misconceptions.description: Believes 0 has a reciprocal (1/0 = 0), and division by zero is fine.
misconceptions.signal: Writes reciprocal tables including 0 → 0.
misconceptions.remedy: Use the defining equation: 0 × ? = 1 has NO solution since 0 times anything is 0. Connect back to why division by zero was undefined for whole numbers.

misconceptions.description: Assumes subtraction and division of rationals are commutative/associative like addition and multiplication.
misconceptions.signal: Rearranges a − b − c freely; claims properties 'hold for all operations'.
misconceptions.remedy: Assign a property-audit: test each property for each operation with small rational values and record the failures (e.g. 1/2 − 1/3 ≠ 1/3 − 1/2). Keep the resulting table for reference.

real_world_hooks: Zooming into a digital map or ruler: always finer marks between marks
Splitting a bill cleverly using distributivity: 7 × ₹99 = 7 × 100 − 7
Temperature scales between two readings — endless in-between values
Photo negatives as 'inverses': undoing an operation to get back to neutral
teaching.video_search: rational numbers properties additive multiplicative inverse density class 8

questions.prompt: What is the additive inverse of −5/7?

options.diagnosis: Gave the number itself; only 0 is its own additive inverse.

questions.explanation: The additive inverse must satisfy (−5/7) + ? = 0, so it is +5/7 — flip the SIGN, not the fraction. Flipping the fraction (7/5 or −7/5) belongs to the multiplicative inverse (reciprocal), a different idea.

questions.prompt: Use a property to evaluate: 3/7 × 5/9 + 3/7 × 4/9

options.diagnosis: Added the 3/7 factor twice as well; the common factor is taken out only once.
Computed the bracket (5/9 + 4/9 = 1) but then dropped the 3/7 multiplier.
Evaluated only the first product and ignored the second term.

questions.explanation: Distributivity in reverse: 3/7 × (5/9 + 4/9) = 3/7 × 9/9 = 3/7 × 1 = 3/7. Spotting the common factor turns two fraction multiplications into none.

questions.prompt: How many rational numbers lie between 1/4 and 1/2?

options.diagnosis: Found one valid in-between number but stopped; averaging can be repeated without end.

options.text: Exactly 25 (the hundredths from 0.26 to 0.49, minus one)

questions.explanation: Between 1/4 and 1/2 lies their average 3/8; between 1/4 and 3/8 lies 5/16; and so on forever. Counting two-decimal-place values (0.26, 0.27, …) misses 0.251, 0.2501, … Rationals are DENSE: no gap is ever empty.

nodes.title: Squares and Square Roots
nodes.description: Perfect squares are numbers like 1, 4, 9, 16 — areas of whole-number squares. You will spot their patterns (unit digits, odd-number sums), find square roots by prime factorisation and by long division, and estimate roots of non-perfect squares. Square roots return in Pythagoras, quadratics and beyond.
learning_outcomes: Can compute squares efficiently and recognise perfect squares up to at least 400
Can use unit-digit and other patterns to rule out non-squares (no perfect square ends in 2, 3, 7 or 8)
Can find square roots by prime factorisation and by the long-division method
Can estimate the square root of a non-perfect square between consecutive integers

misconceptions.description: Distributes the square root over addition: √(a+b) = √a + √b.
misconceptions.remedy: Compute both sides of the claimed identity: √25 = 5 but 3 + 4 = 7 — one counterexample kills the rule. Note the contrast with multiplication, where √(ab) = √a·√b DOES hold.

misconceptions.description: Treats squaring as doubling and square-rooting as halving.
misconceptions.signal: Writes 13² = 26 or √144 = 72.
misconceptions.remedy: Return to the area picture: 13² is the area of a 13×13 grid, wildly more than 26. Keep a doubling column and a squaring column side by side for the same inputs until the difference is vivid.

misconceptions.description: Thinks a perfect square can end in any digit.
misconceptions.signal: Spends time hunting for the square root of numbers ending in 2, 3, 7 or 8.
misconceptions.remedy: Have the student square 0–9 and list the possible unit digits {0,1,4,5,6,9}; use this as a 30-second pre-check before any root-finding.

misconceptions.description: Misplaces the decimal point when squaring decimals: (0.4)² = 1.6 or 0.8.
misconceptions.signal: Decimal squares systematically ×10 too big.
misconceptions.remedy: Route through fractions: (0.4)² = (4/10)² = 16/100 = 0.16. Rule: squaring doubles the number of decimal places. Estimation check: 0.4 < 1, so its square must be SMALLER than 0.4.

real_world_hooks: How many chairs make a perfect square formation for assembly? (arranging 2025 students)
Pixel grids: a 256×256 icon has how many pixels?
Finding the side of a square plot of given area
Chessboard: 64 squares as 8²
teaching.video_search: squares square roots prime factorisation long division method class 8

questions.prompt: What is 13²?

options.diagnosis: Recalled the neighbouring square 14² instead.
Computed 12 × 13 — a near-miss multiplication instead of 13 × 13.

questions.explanation: 13² = 13 × 13 = 169. Squaring means multiplying the number by ITSELF, not by 2: doubling 13 gives only 26.

questions.prompt: What is (0.4)²?

options.diagnosis: Over-shifted: added three decimal places instead of two.

questions.explanation: (0.4)² = 0.4 × 0.4. Digits: 4 × 4 = 16; decimal places: 1 + 1 = 2, giving 0.16. Sense check: 0.4 is less than 1, so its square must be smaller than 0.4 — which rules out both 1.6 and 0.8.

questions.prompt: What is √(9 + 16)?

options.diagnosis: Added correctly but forgot to take the square root at all.

questions.explanation: Add first, THEN take the root: √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5. The tempting shortcut √9 + √16 = 3 + 4 = 7 is wrong — the square root does not distribute over addition. (This is the same trap as (a+b)² ≠ a² + b².)

nodes.title: Cubes and Cube Roots
nodes.description: Cubing a number multiplies it by itself three times — the volume of a cube of that side. You will recognise perfect cubes, use prime factorisation (triples of factors) to find cube roots, and exploit unit-digit patterns for quick mental roots. Unlike squares, cubes of negatives stay negative.
learning_outcomes: Can compute cubes and recognise perfect cubes up to 1000 (and 12³ = 1728)
Can find cube roots by grouping prime factors into triples
Can use unit-digit patterns to find cube roots of perfect cubes mentally
Can explain why cubes of negative numbers are negative, unlike squares

misconceptions.description: Treats cubing as multiplying by 3: 4³ = 12.
misconceptions.signal: Cube answers that are exactly 3× the base.
misconceptions.remedy: Build 4³ from unit cubes (or draw layers): a 4×4×4 block holds 64 cubes, not 12. Keep 'times 3' and 'to the power 3' as a contrasted pair: 4×3 = 12 vs 4³ = 64.

misconceptions.description: Believes the cube of a negative number is positive (over-extending the even-power rule).
misconceptions.signal: Writes (−5)³ = 125.
misconceptions.remedy: Track the signs one product at a time: (−5)(−5) = +25, then (+25)(−5) = −125. Generalise: an ODD count of negative factors leaves a negative product.

misconceptions.description: Finds cube roots by dividing by 3 (or halving), treating the root as inverse of multiplication.
misconceptions.remedy: Emphasise root-as-inverse-of-POWER: ask 'what number, multiplied by itself three times, gives 1728?' and verify candidate answers by cubing them, not by any division.

misconceptions.description: Assumes patterns for squares transfer to cubes (e.g. that cubes cannot end in 2, 3, 7, 8).
misconceptions.signal: Rejects 1728 as a perfect cube 'because it ends in 8'.
misconceptions.remedy: Cube the digits 0–9 and observe: EVERY digit 0–9 appears as a cube's unit digit (8³=512, 3³=27...). This contrast with squares also gives the handy unit-digit map for mental cube roots (2↔8, 3↔7).

real_world_hooks: Rubik's cube: 3×3×3 = 27 cubies
Water tank volumes: a cubical tank of side 2 m holds 8 m³
The Hardy–Ramanujan taxicab number 1729 = 12³ + 1 = 10³ + 9³
Storage boxes: how many 1-cm dice fit in a 5-cm cube?
teaching.video_search: cubes cube roots prime factorisation unit digit trick class 8

questions.prompt: What is 4³?

options.diagnosis: Squared instead of cubing — stopped one multiplication early.
Went one multiplication too far: that is 4⁴.

questions.explanation: 4³ = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 — picture a 4×4×4 stack of unit cubes. Multiplying by the exponent (4 × 3 = 12) is the classic trap.

questions.prompt: Find ∛1728.

options.diagnosis: Halved the number — treating the cube root as division by 2.
Close-recall slip: 13³ = 2197, not 1728. Verify by cubing.

questions.explanation: 1728 = 2⁶ × 3³ = (2² × 3)³, so ∛1728 = 2² × 3 = 12. Check: 12³ = 12 × 12 × 12 = 144 × 12 = 1728 ✓. Dividing 1728 by 3 gives 576 — but roots undo POWERS, not multiplication.

questions.prompt: What is (−5)³?

options.diagnosis: Multiplied by 3 AND lost the sign — two slips stacked.

questions.explanation: (−5)³ = (−5)(−5)(−5) = (+25)(−5) = −125. Three negative factors — an odd count — leave the product negative. Compare (−5)² = +25: only EVEN powers wipe out the sign.

nodes.title: Comparing Quantities: Discounts, Compound Interest
nodes.description: Real prices move in chains: marked price → discount → sales tax/GST → final bill, and savings grow by compound interest, where each year's interest itself earns interest. You will compute successive percentage changes correctly by multiplying growth factors — the single most useful trick in consumer maths.
learning_outcomes: Can compute discount, sale price, and tax/GST on a purchase
Can handle successive percentage changes by multiplying factors (×0.9, ×1.18, …)
Can compute compound interest annually (and half-yearly) using A = P(1 + r/100)ⁿ
Can explain why compound interest exceeds simple interest after the first period

misconceptions.description: Adds successive percentages: a 10% discount followed by 20% is treated as 30% off.
misconceptions.signal: Combines percentage changes by addition regardless of order or base.
misconceptions.remedy: Convert each change to a multiplying factor and compose: ×0.9 then ×0.8 is ×0.72 — a 28% total drop, not 30%. Compute one concrete bill both ways and compare with the till receipt.

misconceptions.description: Computes compound interest as simple interest — interest on the original principal every year.
misconceptions.signal: CI answers equal P×R×T/100; no growth in the yearly interest amounts.
misconceptions.remedy: Build a year-by-year table: year 2's interest is computed on the NEW balance (principal + year-1 interest). Watching the interest column grow (800, 880, 968…) makes compounding concrete.

misconceptions.description: Believes an x% increase then x% decrease (or vice versa) restores the original value.
misconceptions.signal: Says a stock that fell 50% needs only a 50% rise to recover.
misconceptions.remedy: Test with ₹100: −50% → ₹50, then +50% → ₹75. The second change acts on a DIFFERENT base. Generalise via factors: 0.5 × 1.5 = 0.75 ≠ 1.

misconceptions.description: Confuses which price the discount acts on — applies discount percent to cost price or to the sale price instead of the marked price.
misconceptions.signal: Sets up discount = % of SP, or mixes MP, CP and SP freely.
misconceptions.remedy: Draw the price pipeline: MP —discount→ SP —(compare with CP)→ profit. Label every rupee amount in a problem as MP, SP or CP before touching percentages.

real_world_hooks: Festival-sale stacking: '20% off + extra 10% off' — why it isn't 30%
GST at 18% on a restaurant bill after the discount
Fixed deposit vs simple-interest loan from a relative: comparing growth
Population growth of a town at 5% per year — same maths as compound interest
teaching.video_search: successive discounts compound interest formula class 8

questions.prompt: A kurta is marked ₹500 and the shop offers 20% discount. What is the sale price?

options.diagnosis: Computed the discount amount but forgot to subtract it from the marked price.
Treated 20% as ₹20 — subtracted the rate itself instead of 20/100 of the price.
Added the 20% instead of subtracting — direction of a discount reversed.

questions.explanation: Discount = 20% of 500 = ₹100. Sale price = 500 − 100 = ₹400. (Or in one step: 500 × 0.8 = 400.) The discount amount and the price you pay are different answers to different questions.

questions.prompt: A jacket marked ₹800 gets successive discounts of 25% and then 10%. What is the final price?

options.diagnosis: Applied only the 25% discount; the second discount was dropped.
Applied only the 10% discount; the first discount was dropped.

questions.explanation: Multiply the factors: 800 × 0.75 = 600, then 600 × 0.90 = ₹540. Adding the discounts (35% off → ₹520) overstates the saving, because the 10% acts on the already-reduced ₹600, not on ₹800.

questions.prompt: Find the compound interest on ₹8,000 at 10% per annum for 2 years, compounded annually.

options.diagnosis: Reported the final amount A, not the interest A − P.
Computed only the first year's interest.

questions.explanation: A = 8000 × (1.1)² = 8000 × 1.21 = ₹9,680, so CI = 9680 − 8000 = ₹1,680. Simple interest would give 8000×10×2/100 = ₹1,600 — the extra ₹80 is year-2 interest earned ON year-1's ₹800 interest. That is compounding.

nodes.title: Exponents and Powers: Negative Exponents, Scientific Notation
nodes.description: Negative exponents extend the power ladder below 1: 10⁻³ means 1/10³, letting scientific notation describe the very small (a bacterium's width) as easily as the very large. You will apply all the exponent laws with integer exponents and convert numbers to and from standard form in both directions.
learning_outcomes: Can evaluate powers with negative integer exponents via a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ
Can apply the laws of exponents across integer exponents, including a⁰ = 1
Can write very small numbers in standard form k × 10⁻ⁿ and convert back
Can compare magnitudes expressed in scientific notation

misconceptions.description: Thinks a negative exponent makes the VALUE negative: 2⁻³ = −8.
misconceptions.signal: Treats the minus in the exponent as the sign of the answer.
misconceptions.remedy: Walk the ladder downward: 2² = 4, 2¹ = 2, 2⁰ = 1, 2⁻¹ = 1/2, 2⁻² = 1/4 — each step divides by 2 and the values stay POSITIVE, just small. Negative exponent = reciprocal, not negative number.

misconceptions.description: Divides exponents when dividing powers: a⁸ ÷ a² = a⁴.
misconceptions.signal: Quotient-law answers with divided instead of subtracted exponents.
misconceptions.remedy: Expand once: (a·a·a·a·a·a·a·a)/(a·a) cancels two factors leaving six, so a⁶ — the exponents SUBTRACT. Derive, then drill the law with cases where subtracting and dividing differ.

misconceptions.description: Gets the sign of the exponent wrong in standard form: writes small numbers with positive powers (0.00052 = 5.2 × 10⁴).
misconceptions.signal: Standard-form conversions of decimals below 1 carry positive exponents, or vice versa.
misconceptions.remedy: Anchor the rule in size: numbers ≥ 1 need positive powers, numbers between 0 and 1 need negative powers. Always multiply back to check: 5.2 × 10⁴ = 52,000, clearly not 0.00052.

misconceptions.description: Counts decimal shifts off by one when converting to scientific notation (counting zeros instead of shifts).
misconceptions.signal: Answers like 5.2 × 10⁻⁵ for 0.00052; consistently one power out.
misconceptions.remedy: Standardise the procedure: move the point until exactly one nonzero digit is left of it, COUNTING each hop. For 0.00052 the point hops 4 places right, so 10⁻⁴. Verify by shifting back.

real_world_hooks: Size of a red blood cell (≈ 7 × 10⁻⁶ m) vs distance to the Moon (≈ 3.84 × 10⁸ m)
Mobile data units: 1 KB, 1 MB, 1 GB as powers of 10 (and of 2)
A virus vs a cricket ball: how many powers of ten apart?
Interest rates and probabilities written as 10⁻² scale numbers
teaching.video_search: negative exponents scientific notation standard form small numbers class 8

questions.prompt: What is 2⁻³?

options.diagnosis: Computed 1/(2×3) — multiplied base by exponent instead of raising to the power.

questions.explanation: A negative exponent means reciprocal: 2⁻³ = 1/2³ = 1/8. The result is a small POSITIVE number — the minus sign moves the power downstairs; it never makes the value negative.

questions.prompt: Simplify: 5⁸ ÷ 5²

options.diagnosis: Divided the bases (5 ÷ 5 = 1) as well as handling exponents — the base stays 5.
Added the exponents — that is the rule for MULTIPLYING powers, not dividing.

questions.explanation: Dividing same-base powers subtracts exponents: 5⁸ ÷ 5² = 5⁸⁻² = 5⁶. Expanding shows why: eight 5s over two 5s cancels to six 5s. Dividing the exponents (8 ÷ 2 = 4) is the classic wrong move.

questions.prompt: Write 0.00052 in standard form.

options.diagnosis: Equal in value but not standard form — the leading factor must be at least 1 and less than 10.

questions.explanation: Move the decimal point 4 places right to get 5.2, so 0.00052 = 5.2 × 10⁻⁴. The exponent is negative because the number is less than 1, and it is 4 (not 5) because the point hops four places. Check: 5.2 ÷ 10⁴ = 0.00052 ✓.

nodes.title: Direct and Inverse Proportion
nodes.description: Two quantities are in direct proportion when their RATIO stays constant (double one, double the other) and in inverse proportion when their PRODUCT stays constant (double one, halve the other). The crucial skill is deciding which model — if either — fits a situation before computing.
learning_outcomes: Can test whether tabled data shows direct proportion (y/x constant) or inverse proportion (xy constant)
Can solve direct-proportion problems via the constant ratio or unitary method
Can solve inverse-proportion problems (workers–days, speed–time) via the constant product
Can identify situations that are NEITHER kind of proportion (e.g. age vs height)

misconceptions.description: Applies direct proportion everywhere, including to inverse situations: 'more workers, so multiply the days up'.
misconceptions.signal: Worker/speed problems answered with the quantities scaling the same way; more workers 'take longer'.
misconceptions.remedy: Install a direction check before any computation: 'if this goes UP, does that go UP or DOWN?' Sketch the situation (more taps filling a tank faster) and only then pick the model.

misconceptions.description: Handles inverse proportion additively: 2 more workers means 2 fewer days.
misconceptions.signal: Answers offset by a fixed difference rather than scaled by a factor.
misconceptions.remedy: Use the constant-product frame explicitly: total work = workers × days stays FIXED (6 × 12 = 72 worker-days), so 8 workers need 72 ÷ 8 = 9 days, not 10. Tabulate several (workers, days) pairs and watch the product.

misconceptions.description: Treats direct proportion as an additive relationship: y = x + k instead of y = kx.
misconceptions.signal: Extends tables by adding the same gap (4→12 becomes 10→18 'because +8').
misconceptions.remedy: Test the additive rule at zero: 0 cups of rice would still 'serve 8 people' under +8 — absurd. Check y/x down a real table to reveal the multiplicative constant.

misconceptions.description: In inverse proportion, keeps the RATIO constant instead of the product.
misconceptions.signal: Sets up y₁/x₁ = y₂/x₂ for speed–time problems.
misconceptions.remedy: Contrast the two set-ups on the same problem and check which answer respects reality (faster speed must give LESS time). Memorise the pairings: direct ↔ equal ratios; inverse ↔ equal products.

real_world_hooks: Petrol and distance: double the fuel, double the kilometres (direct)
Workers building a wall, or pipes filling a tank (inverse)
Speed vs journey time to school (inverse)
Recipe quantities per guest (direct) — and why cooking TIME is not proportional to guests
teaching.video_search: direct and inverse proportion word problems class 8

questions.prompt: x and y are in DIRECT proportion, and when x = 4, y = 12. What is y when x = 10?

options.diagnosis: Multiplied 10 × 12 without using the given pair — no proportional set-up at all.

questions.explanation: Direct proportion keeps y/x constant: y/x = 12/4 = 3, so y = 3 × 10 = 30. The answer 18 comes from the additive pattern '+8', which fails the ratio test (18/10 ≠ 3); 4.8 keeps the product constant, which is the INVERSE model.

questions.prompt: 6 workers can finish a job in 12 days. How long will 8 workers take, working at the same rate?

options.diagnosis: Adjusted in the wrong direction — ADDED days when more workers must reduce them.

questions.explanation: Total work = 6 × 12 = 72 worker-days (constant product). With 8 workers: 72 ÷ 8 = 9 days. Direct-proportion setup gives 16 days — but more workers taking LONGER fails the common-sense direction check.

questions.prompt: A car covers a fixed route in 3 hours at 60 km/h. How long does the same route take at 90 km/h?

options.diagnosis: Assumed 1.5× speed simply halves the time; the factor is 60/90 = 2/3, not 1/2.

questions.explanation: The distance is fixed: 60 × 3 = 180 km. At 90 km/h, time = 180 ÷ 90 = 2 hours. Speed and time are inversely proportional (constant product 180), so time scales by 60/90 = 2/3: 3 × 2/3 = 2 h.

nodes.title: Playing with Numbers: General Form and Divisibility
nodes.description: Writing a two-digit number as 10a + b turns number tricks into algebra: you can PROVE why ab + ba is always divisible by 11, justify the divisibility tests for 3 and 9, and crack letter-for-digit puzzles. This chapter is a first taste of proof through generalisation.
learning_outcomes: Can express 2- and 3-digit numbers in general form (10a + b, 100a + 10b + c)
Can prove simple facts like 11 | (ab + ba) and 9 | (abc − cba variants) using the general form
Can justify the divisibility tests for 2, 3, 5, 9 and 10 from place value
Can solve letter-digit (cryptarithm) puzzles using digit constraints

misconceptions.description: Reads the two-digit numeral 'ab' as the product a × b instead of 10a + b.
misconceptions.signal: Substitutes ab = 6 when a = 2, b = 3 (instead of 23).
misconceptions.remedy: Expand notation aloud: the NUMERAL ab means 'a tens and b ones' = 10a + b; contrast with the algebra product ab = a×b. Use an overbar or colour for numeral-form until the distinction is stable.

misconceptions.description: Checks divisibility by 3 or 9 with the last digit, or believes a 9 anywhere in the number guarantees divisibility by 9.
misconceptions.signal: Says 19 is divisible by 9 'because it ends in 9'.
misconceptions.remedy: Derive the digit-sum test from general form: 10a + b = 9a + (a + b) — the 9a part is always divisible by 9, so everything hinges on the digit SUM. Test on 19 (1+9=10, not divisible).

misconceptions.description: Believes divisibility by 3 implies divisibility by 9.
misconceptions.signal: Concludes 9 | 12 or 9 | 15 after passing the '3' test.
misconceptions.remedy: Line up counterexamples (12, 15, 21 — divisible by 3, not 9) and show the containment goes the OTHER way: every multiple of 9 is a multiple of 3, not vice versa. Venn-diagram the two sets.

misconceptions.description: In digit puzzles, forgets digit constraints: lets a letter be more than 9, ignores carries, or allows a leading digit to be 0.
misconceptions.signal: Puzzle 'solutions' with impossible digits or unverified columns.
misconceptions.remedy: Solve column by column with explicit carry bookkeeping, then ALWAYS substitute the found digits back into the original sum to verify.

real_world_hooks: Number magic tricks: 'reverse and add' party tricks explained
Why the digit-sum trick for checking bills and roll-number sums works
Cryptic puzzles and escape-room codes as cryptarithms
Bank card checksums: real systems built on divisibility
teaching.video_search: general form of numbers divisibility proofs letter digit puzzles class 8

questions.prompt: A two-digit number has tens digit a and units digit b. Its value is:

options.diagnosis: Added the digits — that gives the digit sum, not the number.
Swapped the place values: this is the number with its digits REVERSED.

questions.explanation: The tens digit contributes ten times its face value: the number is 10a + b. For a = 2, b = 3 that is 23 — while a × b = 6, a + b = 5 and 10b + a = 32, all different things.

questions.prompt: For what digit x is the number 52x3 divisible by 9?

options.diagnosis: Assumed the existing digits already worked; their sum is 10, which is not a multiple of 9.

questions.explanation: Digit sum = 5 + 2 + x + 3 = 10 + x. For divisibility by 9 the sum must be a multiple of 9, so 10 + x = 18, giving x = 8. Note x = 2 makes the sum 12 — divisible by 3 but NOT by 9.

questions.prompt: In the puzzle A + A + A = BA (a two-digit number whose units digit is again A), what digit is A?

options.diagnosis: 0+0+0 = 0 is a single digit, not a two-digit number BA — the trivial case doesn't satisfy the puzzle.

questions.explanation: We need 3A to be a two-digit number ending in A: 3 × 5 = 15 ends in 5 ✓, so A = 5 and B = 1 (5+5+5 = 15). Check the others: 3×6 = 18 ends in 8, 3×2 = 6 isn't two-digit — verifying the units-digit condition is the step most solvers skip.

nodes.title: Linear Equations in One Variable: Variables on Both Sides
nodes.description: Equations now carry the variable on BOTH sides (2x + 5 = x + 9), and may involve fractions or expressions that need simplifying first. You will reduce them systematically to x = value, and use them to crack age, number, perimeter and money problems.
learning_outcomes: Can solve linear equations with variables on both sides
Can clear fractions by multiplying EVERY term by the common denominator
Can reduce word problems (ages, numbers, money) to linear equations and solve them
Can verify solutions by substitution and interpret them in context

misconceptions.description: Transposes constants without inverting the operation: from 2x + 5 = x + 9 gets x = 9 + 5.
misconceptions.signal: Constants cross the equals sign with their signs unchanged.
misconceptions.remedy: Slow down to both-sides moves: subtract 5 from both sides and WATCH it become −5 on the right. Require the check-by-substitution step, which exposes the error immediately (14 + 5 ≠ ...).

misconceptions.description: Moves variable terms across without changing sign: 2x + 5 = x + 9 becomes 2x + x = 9 − 5.
misconceptions.signal: Variable terms collected by ADDING coefficients that should subtract.
misconceptions.remedy: Treat x-terms exactly like number terms: subtract x from both sides explicitly. Colour-code x-terms and constants and move one colour at a time, writing every intermediate line.

misconceptions.description: When clearing fractions or brackets, multiplies only the fraction term, not EVERY term.
misconceptions.signal: From x/3 + 5 = 8 writes x + 5 = 24.
misconceptions.remedy: Draw the multiplication as distributing over the whole side: 3(x/3 + 5) = 3×8 forces 3×5 too. Alternatively isolate the fraction first (x/3 = 3) so only one multiplication is ever needed.

misconceptions.description: Stops mid-solution (reports 4x = 56 as the answer) or answers a different unknown than the one asked.
misconceptions.signal: Final line is not of the form x = …, or gives the mother's age when the child's was asked.
misconceptions.remedy: End every solution with two rituals: (1) reduce to x = value, (2) re-read the question and answer THAT sentence in words ('Sahil is 14').

real_world_hooks: Two mobile plans reaching equal cost: 99 + 2x = 149 + x
Age puzzles across years: 'in 5 years the sum of our ages…'
Splitting prize money in a given ratio with a fixed bonus
Balancing weights on a two-pan scale with unknown packets on both pans
teaching.video_search: linear equations variables on both sides word problems class 8

questions.prompt: Solve: 2x + 5 = x + 9

options.diagnosis: Sign flipped in the final step; substitute back to catch it: 2(−4)+5 = −3 ≠ 5.

questions.explanation: Subtract x from both sides: x + 5 = 9. Subtract 5: x = 4. Check: 2(4)+5 = 13 and 4+9 = 13 ✓. Moving 5 across unchanged gives x = 14, whose check fails (33 ≠ 23) — always substitute back.

questions.prompt: Solve: x/3 + 5 = 8

options.diagnosis: Divided by 3 at the end instead of multiplying — inverse operation inverted.

questions.explanation: Isolate the fraction: x/3 = 8 − 5 = 3. Multiply both sides by 3: x = 9. Check: 9/3 + 5 = 8 ✓. Multiplying through by 3 but forgetting the 5 gives x + 5 = 24 → 19, and stopping at x/3 = 3 gives the unfinished '3'.

questions.prompt: Sahil is x years old and his mother is 3x years old. In 5 years, the sum of their ages will be 66. How old is Sahil NOW?
questions.explanation: In 5 years: (x+5) + (3x+5) = 66, so 4x + 10 = 66, 4x = 56, x = 14. Check: ages now 14 and 42; in five years 19 + 47 = 66 ✓. Forgetting the two +5s gives 4x = 66 → 16.5; '42' answers the mother's age; '56' stops at 4x.

nodes.title: Algebraic Expressions and Identities
nodes.description: You will multiply monomials, binomials and polynomials, and meet the standard identities: (a+b)² = a²+2ab+b², (a−b)² = a²−2ab+b², and (a+b)(a−b) = a²−b². Identities are equalities true for ALL values — and they turn ugly arithmetic like 103² into two-second mental maths.
learning_outcomes: Can multiply monomials and binomials, applying exponent rules to variables
Can expand using the three standard identities and recognise when they apply
Can distinguish an identity (true for all values) from an equation (true for some)
Can use identities for fast numeric computation (103², 98², 52 × 48)

misconceptions.description: Squares a sum term by term: (a+b)² = a² + b².
misconceptions.signal: The middle term 2ab never appears; 103² computed as 100² + 3².
misconceptions.remedy: Draw the (a+b)×(a+b) area square: it visibly contains a², b² AND two ab rectangles. Numerically test a = b = 1: (1+1)² = 4 but 1² + 1² = 2. Keep the picture on the wall until 2ab is automatic.

misconceptions.description: Extends the same error to differences: (a−b)² = a² − b², or muddles the sign of the middle term.
misconceptions.signal: Expansions of (a−b)² missing +b² or with −b²; middle term sign random.
misconceptions.remedy: Expand (a−b)(a−b) longhand once, tracking each of the four products with its sign: −ab appears twice (giving −2ab) and (−b)(−b) = +b². The LAST term of a square is always positive.

misconceptions.description: Multiplies binomials by pairing only firsts and lasts: (x+2)(x+3) = x² + 6.
misconceptions.signal: Products of binomials with two terms instead of (up to) four.
misconceptions.remedy: Use the 2×2 grid (area) method so all FOUR partial products get a cell; only then compress to the shortcut. Check by substituting x = 1: (3)(4) = 12 but 1 + 6 = 7.

misconceptions.description: Mishandles variables when multiplying monomials: 3x × 4x = 12x (or 7x²).
misconceptions.signal: Coefficients handled but exponents not added, or coefficients added while variables multiplied.
misconceptions.remedy: Split every product into (numbers) × (letters): 3x·4x = (3·4)(x·x) = 12x². Multiply coefficients, ADD exponents — rehearse the two rules as separate moves.

real_world_hooks: Mental-math party trick: 103² or 98 × 102 in your head via identities
Area of a square field extended by b metres on each side — where 2ab lives
Framing a square photo: the border area IS (a+b)² − a²
Quick checks for shop bills: 52 × 48 = 50² − 2²
teaching.video_search: algebraic identities a plus b whole square expansion area model class 8

questions.prompt: Multiply: 3x × 4x²

options.diagnosis: Added the coefficients instead of multiplying them (exponents handled correctly).

questions.explanation: Group numbers and letters: (3 × 4) × (x × x²) = 12x³. Coefficients multiply (3×4 = 12); exponents of the same base ADD (1 + 2 = 3).

questions.prompt: Expand: (x + 2)(x + 3)

options.diagnosis: Dropped the constant product 2 × 3 — three of the four partial products kept.
Swapped the roles of sum and product: the x-coefficient is 2+3 and the constant is 2×3, not the other way round.

questions.explanation: Four products: x·x + x·3 + 2·x + 2·3 = x² + 3x + 2x + 6 = x² + 5x + 6. Check at x = 1: (3)(4) = 12 and 1 + 5 + 6 = 12 ✓. Multiplying only 'firsts and lasts' loses the two middle products.

questions.prompt: Use an identity to evaluate 103².

options.diagnosis: Computed a² + 2ab but dropped the final b² = 9.
Used ab instead of 2ab for the middle term — halved the cross term.

questions.explanation: 103² = (100 + 3)² = 100² + 2(100)(3) + 3² = 10000 + 600 + 9 = 10609. Leaving out the cross term 2ab (giving 10009) is exactly the (a+b)² = a² + b² fallacy — the area model shows the two missing 100×3 rectangles.

nodes.title: Factorisation of Algebraic Expressions
nodes.description: Factorisation reverses expansion: rewriting an expression as a product of factors. You will take out common factors, regroup, apply the identities backwards (a² − b² = (a+b)(a−b)), split the middle term of x² + bx + c, and divide expressions cleanly — with a spotlight on the cancellation errors everyone must unlearn.
learning_outcomes: Can factor out the greatest common monomial factor completely
Can factorise using identities, especially the difference of squares
Can factorise trinomials x² + bx + c by splitting the middle term
Can divide a polynomial by a monomial correctly, term by term

misconceptions.description: Treats a difference of squares as the square of a difference: a² − b² = (a − b)².
misconceptions.signal: Factors x² − 25 as (x − 5)².
misconceptions.remedy: Expand (x−5)² = x² − 10x + 25 and compare with x² − 25 — the middle term betrays the difference. Verify the correct factorisation numerically: at x = 6, x² − 25 = 11 = (6+5)(6−5) ✓.

misconceptions.description: Cancels single terms across addition in a fraction: (5x + 10)/5 = x + 10.
misconceptions.signal: Cancellation strikes through one term of a sum while other terms ride along untouched.
misconceptions.remedy: Factor BEFORE cancelling: (5x + 10)/5 = 5(x + 2)/5 = x + 2. Rule: only common FACTORS of the whole numerator and denominator cancel. Numeric check at x = 1: 15/5 = 3 = 1 + 2 ✓, not 11.

misconceptions.description: Factors incompletely or unevenly — divides only some terms by the common factor: 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 9).
misconceptions.signal: One term inside the bracket unchanged; expansion of the answer doesn't return the original.
misconceptions.remedy: Institute the expand-back check: multiply the factored form out and compare with the original expression, every single time. Divide each term by the common factor in writing.

misconceptions.description: When splitting the middle term of x² + bx + c, hunts for numbers with sum c and product b (roles swapped).
misconceptions.signal: x² + 5x + 6 factored as (x + 1)(x + 5) or similar.
misconceptions.remedy: Anchor with expansion: (x+p)(x+q) = x² + (p+q)x + pq — SUM goes with x, PRODUCT is the constant. Practise listing factor pairs of c first, then testing their sums against b.

real_world_hooks: Un-multiplying: finding the dimensions of a rectangular plot from its area expression
Simplifying a formula before coding it into a spreadsheet
Splitting a bill of (5x + 10) rupees equally among 5 friends
teaching.video_search: factorisation common factors identities splitting middle term class 8

questions.prompt: Factorise: 6x + 9

options.diagnosis: Took out 6, but 9 is not divisible by 6 — expanding gives 6x + 18, not 6x + 9.
Took x common from a term that has no x; expanding gives 15x.

questions.explanation: HCF of 6x and 9 is 3: 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3). Always expand back to check: 3 × 2x + 3 × 3 = 6x + 9 ✓. In 3(2x + 9) the second term was never divided by 3.

questions.prompt: Factorise: x² − 25
questions.explanation: Difference of squares: x² − 5² = (x + 5)(x − 5). Both square options fail the expansion check — (x−5)² = x² − 10x + 25 has a middle term that x² − 25 lacks. And x(x − 25) = x² − 25x, also wrong.

questions.prompt: Simplify: (5x + 10) ÷ 5

options.diagnosis: Combined 5x and 10 into 15x first — unlike terms cannot be added.

questions.explanation: Factor first: (5x + 10)/5 = 5(x + 2)/5 = x + 2 — EVERY term gets divided by 5. Cancelling the 5 against only one term gives x + 10 or 5x + 2; test x = 1: (15)/5 = 3, and only x + 2 gives 3.

nodes.title: Introduction to Graphs: Coordinates and Linear Graphs
nodes.description: The coordinate plane turns pairs of numbers into points and relationships into pictures. You will plot points, read line graphs, and draw the graphs of simple linear relationships like y = 2x — seeing for the first time that an equation IS a line. This bridge between algebra and geometry carries all of higher mathematics.
learning_outcomes: Can plot and read points (x, y), respecting the order of coordinates
Can locate points on the axes and state where axis points belong
Can check whether a point lies on the graph of a simple equation like y = 2x
Can interpret real line graphs (distance–time, cost–quantity) including rates as steepness

misconceptions.description: Ignores coordinate order: treats (3, 5) and (5, 3) as the same point.
misconceptions.signal: Plots x along the vertical axis at random; swapped points 'look fine'.
misconceptions.remedy: Fix the convention with the corridor-then-stairs story: along the corridor (x) FIRST, then up the stairs (y). Plot both (3,5) and (5,3) on one grid to see they are genuinely different places.

misconceptions.description: Misplaces axis points: thinks (0, 4) lies on the x-axis (matching the '0' with 'x').
misconceptions.signal: Points with a zero coordinate put on the wrong axis.
misconceptions.remedy: Reason by movement, not by symbol-matching: (0, 4) means move 0 along x — you stay put — then 4 up: you land ON the y-axis. Generalise: x = 0 IS the y-axis, y = 0 is the x-axis.

misconceptions.description: Believes only the plotted/tabled points belong to a line's graph — points in between 'don't count'.
misconceptions.signal: Denies that (1.5, 3) lies on y = 2x after plotting only integer points.
misconceptions.remedy: Zoom in: check (1.5, 3) in the equation (3 = 2 × 1.5 ✓) and plot it — it lands exactly on the line. The line is the set of ALL solutions, a continuous infinity of points.

misconceptions.description: Reads graphs without attending to axis labels or scales — comparing steepness across different scales, or joining discrete data meaninglessly.
