misconceptions.signal: Concludes 'faster' from a steeper look alone; connects favourite-fruit bar categories with a line.
misconceptions.remedy: Always read the axes aloud first (units and scale). Show the same data plotted at two scales, and discuss when joining points means something (continuous quantities) and when it doesn't.

real_world_hooks: Battleship-style grid games: coordinates as addresses
Distance–time graph of your school bus with its stops (flat parts!)
Cinema seat numbers row-and-seat as ordered pairs
Mobile recharge: talktime vs amount as a straight line through the origin
teaching.video_search: coordinate plane plotting points linear graphs introduction class 8

questions.prompt: Where does the point (0, −4) lie?

options.diagnosis: Any zero coordinate read as 'the origin'; the origin is only (0, 0).
Points ON an axis belong to no quadrant; movement along x is zero here.

questions.explanation: From the origin, move 0 units horizontally (stay on the vertical axis), then 4 units DOWN. The point sits on the y-axis below the origin. Every point with x-coordinate 0 lies on the y-axis.

questions.prompt: Which point lies on the graph of y = 2x?

options.diagnosis: Treated 'y = 2x' as 'y = x + 2' — added 2 instead of doubling.
Satisfies x = 2y — the relationship was inverted (halving instead of doubling).

questions.explanation: Substitute: for (3, 6), y = 2x gives 6 = 2 × 3 ✓. For (6, 3): 3 ≠ 12 — swapping coordinates breaks the equation. A point lies on a graph exactly when its coordinates satisfy the equation.

questions.prompt: A distance–time graph shows a cyclist moving in a straight line from (0 h, 0 km) to (2 h, 20 km). What is the cyclist's speed?

options.diagnosis: Inverted the slope: computed hours per kilometre instead of kilometres per hour.
Multiplied distance by time instead of dividing.

questions.explanation: Speed = distance ÷ time = 20 km ÷ 2 h = 10 km/h — the slope (steepness) of the line. Reading the end value 20 as the speed ignores the time axis; slope always needs BOTH axes.

nodes.title: Understanding Quadrilaterals: Polygon Angle Sums and Parallelograms
nodes.description: The interior angles of an n-sided polygon sum to (n−2)×180°, while exterior angles always total 360°. You will use these facts, then dive into the parallelogram family — opposite sides and angles equal, diagonals bisecting each other — and see how rectangle, rhombus and square refine it step by step.
learning_outcomes: Can compute interior angle sums of polygons via (n−2) × 180° and use the 360° exterior-angle fact
Can use parallelogram properties (opposite sides/angles equal, adjacent angles supplementary, diagonals bisect each other) to find unknowns
Can state which extra properties rectangles, rhombuses and squares add
Can place the special quadrilaterals in a correct hierarchy

misconceptions.description: Uses 360° as the interior angle sum of EVERY polygon, not just quadrilaterals.
misconceptions.signal: Pentagon angle problems solved with 360°; answers systematically 180° short per extra side.
misconceptions.remedy: Triangulate polygons from one vertex: a pentagon splits into 3 triangles, so 3 × 180° = 540°. Build the (n−2) pattern from a table of n = 3, 4, 5, 6 rather than as a bare formula.

misconceptions.description: Believes the diagonals of every parallelogram are equal (importing the rectangle's special property).
misconceptions.signal: Claims diagonals equal in a generic parallelogram or rhombus.
misconceptions.remedy: Measure the diagonals of a drawn slanted parallelogram — visibly unequal. Sort diagonal properties into a table: bisect each other (all parallelograms) vs equal (rectangles/squares) vs perpendicular (rhombus/square).

misconceptions.description: Thinks adjacent angles of a parallelogram are equal (instead of supplementary), confusing them with opposite angles.
misconceptions.signal: Given one angle 70°, writes the neighbouring angle as 70°.
misconceptions.remedy: Walk the parallel-lines connection: adjacent angles are co-interior angles between parallel sides, so they sum to 180°; OPPOSITE angles are the equal pair. Colour opposite angle pairs identically in diagrams.

misconceptions.description: Gets the quadrilateral hierarchy backwards: 'every rectangle is a square', or refuses 'a square is a rhombus'.
misconceptions.signal: Hierarchy questions answered by visual prototype rather than property lists.
misconceptions.remedy: Run each shape through property checklists: a square passes ALL rhombus tests (four equal sides) and all rectangle tests (four right angles). Draw the family tree with arrows meaning 'is a special kind of'.

real_world_hooks: Sliding gates and scissor lifts: parallelogram linkages in action
Why mobile screens and doors are rectangles — equal diagonals as a squareness check used by carpenters
Kite festival: the geometric kite and its diagonals
Floor tiles: which polygons tile because of their angle sums?
teaching.video_search: polygon angle sum parallelogram properties rectangle rhombus square hierarchy class 8

questions.prompt: What is the sum of the interior angles of a pentagon?

options.diagnosis: Used n instead of n−2 (or the hexagon's count) in (n−2) × 180°.
Estimated 100° per angle × 5 — plausible-looking but not a polygon fact.

questions.explanation: A pentagon splits into 5 − 2 = 3 triangles from one vertex, so its angles total 3 × 180° = 540°. The 360° figure is the QUADRILATERAL sum (and, separately, every polygon's EXTERIOR angle total).

questions.prompt: In a parallelogram, one angle measures 70°. What is the measure of the angle ADJACENT to it?

options.diagnosis: Subtracted from 90° — complement used where a supplement is needed.
Subtracted from 360°, the full quadrilateral sum, instead of from 180°.

questions.explanation: Adjacent angles of a parallelogram lie between the two parallel sides (co-interior), so they are supplementary: 180 − 70 = 110°. It is the OPPOSITE angle that equals 70°.

questions.prompt: Which quadrilateral always has diagonals that are EQUAL and bisect each other, without needing all four sides equal?

options.diagnosis: A general trapezium's diagonals are neither equal nor mutually bisecting — property list not checked.

questions.explanation: All parallelograms have diagonals that bisect each other, but EQUAL diagonals is the rectangle's special extra (from its right angles). A rhombus instead has perpendicular diagonals — equal only when it becomes a square. Carpenters exploit this: equal diagonals certify right angles.

nodes.title: Practical Geometry: Constructing Quadrilaterals
nodes.description: A quadrilateral needs five independent measurements to be pinned down — four sides alone leave it floppy. You will construct quadrilaterals from five given parts (e.g. four sides and a diagonal) by splitting them into two triangles, reusing everything you know about triangle construction.
learning_outcomes: Can explain why 5 measurements (suitably chosen) determine a quadrilateral while 4 do not
Can construct quadrilaterals given: 4 sides + 1 diagonal; 3 sides + 2 diagonals; 2 adjacent sides + 3 angles; 3 sides + 2 included angles
Can decompose the construction into two triangle constructions sharing a diagonal
Can detect impossible data (triangle inequality failing inside a component triangle)

misconceptions.description: Believes four sides determine a quadrilateral uniquely, as three sides do a triangle.
misconceptions.signal: Constructs from 4 sides only and is surprised the shape can be 'squashed' into different quadrilaterals.
misconceptions.remedy: Build a four-strip hinged frame (or straw model) and squash it: same four sides, many shapes. Contrast with a triangle frame, which cannot flex — rigidity needs the fifth measurement (a diagonal or angle).

misconceptions.description: Thinks ANY five measurements will do, regardless of which parts they are.
misconceptions.signal: Attempts constructions from data like four angles + one side, or five angles, and stalls.
misconceptions.remedy: Classify the workable data sets and trace each back to two constructible triangles. Show a failing case (four angles already forced by the 360° sum, so they carry less information).

misconceptions.description: Ignores feasibility checks: starts drawing without testing the triangle inequality in each half-triangle.
misconceptions.signal: Arcs fail to intersect mid-construction; student blames drawing accuracy rather than the data.
misconceptions.remedy: Before drawing, split the data into its two triangles and verify each satisfies the triangle inequality. Turn 'my compass slipped' moments into data-checking moments.

misconceptions.description: Draws by eye and adjusts: places vertices where they 'look right' instead of at arc intersections.
misconceptions.signal: No construction arcs visible; measurements of the finished figure drift from the given data.
misconceptions.remedy: Require all arcs to remain visible in submitted work and have students measure their own finished figure against the specification — accuracy becomes checkable, not aesthetic.

real_world_hooks: Why gates and grills get a diagonal brace — the fifth measurement in steel
Land records: a four-sided plot needs a diagonal measure to be mapped exactly
Foldable furniture and collapsible stalls: useful floppiness of 4-bar frames
Kite-making: fixing a quadrilateral's shape with its two diagonal sticks
teaching.video_search: constructing quadrilaterals four sides diagonal compass class 8

questions.prompt: How many measurements are needed, in general, to construct a unique quadrilateral?

options.diagnosis: Carried over the triangle's count; a quadrilateral has more independent parts to fix.

options.text: 8 (all four sides and all four angles)
options.diagnosis: That is every part — far more than needed; five suitably chosen parts suffice.

questions.explanation: Four sides leave a quadrilateral hinged and floppy — it can flex into infinitely many shapes. One more suitable measurement (say a diagonal) locks it, because the diagonal splits it into two rigid triangles. Hence 5.

questions.prompt: To construct quadrilateral ABCD given the four sides and the diagonal AC, the standard strategy is to:

options.text: Construct triangle ABC first, then triangle ACD on the same base AC
Draw the four sides in order and adjust until the figure closes
Begin by drawing all four angles
Draw both diagonals first and hang the sides on them
options.diagnosis: Only ONE diagonal is given; the second diagonal's length is an outcome, not data.

questions.explanation: The diagonal AC splits ABCD into triangles ABC (sides AB, BC, AC) and ACD (sides AC, CD, DA) — each constructible by SSS. Building two triangles on the shared base AC assembles the quadrilateral exactly.

questions.prompt: You are asked to construct quadrilateral ABCD with AB = 4 cm, BC = 5 cm and diagonal AC = 10 cm (plus suitable remaining data). What do you conclude?

options.text: The construction is impossible: in triangle ABC, AB + BC = 9 < 10 = AC
It must be possible, since five measurements are provided
It is possible if drawn very carefully with a sharp pencil
It is impossible because a diagonal can never be the longest given length
options.diagnosis: Right verdict, wrong rule — diagonals CAN be longest; the actual test is the triangle inequality.

questions.explanation: Triangle ABC must be built from sides 4, 5 and 10 — but 4 + 5 = 9 < 10 violates the triangle inequality, so the arcs can never meet. Five measurements only suffice when each component triangle is actually constructible.

nodes.title: Visualising Solid Shapes: Views and Euler's Relation
nodes.description: You will map solids from different viewpoints (top, front, side), read simple maps, and discover Euler's beautiful relation for polyhedra: F + V − E = 2 — faces plus vertices minus edges equals two, for EVERY polyhedron from a cube to a football. It is many students' first universal theorem about 3D space.
learning_outcomes: Can draw and match top, front and side views of solids and cube arrangements
Can distinguish polyhedra (flat faces) from non-polyhedra (cylinder, sphere, cone)
Can verify Euler's relation F + V − E = 2 on prisms and pyramids
Can use Euler's relation to find a missing count (e.g. faces from V and E)

misconceptions.description: Misremembers or distrusts Euler's relation: uses F + V − E = 0, F = V + E − 2, or believes the value changes from solid to solid.
misconceptions.signal: Plugs counts into a scrambled formula; answers 'it depends on the shape' for F + V − E.
misconceptions.remedy: Build a data table (cube, cuboid, triangular prism, square pyramid, tetrahedron) and compute F + V − E for each — the constant 2 emerges from the student's own data, then the formula is remembered as a discovered fact.

misconceptions.description: Confuses which view is which: expects the top view of a cylinder to be a rectangle, or draws the front view from above.
misconceptions.signal: Views swapped or blended; the same drawing offered for top and front.
misconceptions.remedy: Physically move: hold the object at eye level for the front view, then look straight down for the top view. Use a torch to cast the corresponding shadows and match each to its name.

misconceptions.description: Applies Euler's relation to non-polyhedra (cylinder, cone, sphere) or counts curved surfaces as 'faces'.
misconceptions.signal: Reports F + V − E ≠ 2 for a cylinder as a 'violation', counting its curved surface as a face.
misconceptions.remedy: Define polyhedron sharply: flat polygonal faces, straight edges. Sort solids into polyhedra / non-polyhedra BEFORE any counting; Euler's relation applies only to the first pile.

misconceptions.description: Miscounts hidden faces, edges or vertices when working from a 2D sketch.
misconceptions.signal: Counts of F, E, V systematically low; only visible parts tallied.
misconceptions.remedy: Count on a real model with a marker — tick each face/edge/vertex as it is counted. On sketches, draw hidden edges dashed and count the dashes too.

real_world_hooks: Building plans: floor plan (top view) vs elevation (front view) of a house
A football's pentagon-hexagon pattern satisfies F + V − E = 2
Minecraft-style block builds: drawing their three views
Reading a metro map vs an aerial photo — maps as chosen views
teaching.video_search: views of 3d shapes euler formula polyhedron F V E class 8

questions.prompt: For any polyhedron, F + V − E equals:
questions.explanation: Euler's relation: F + V − E = 2 for every polyhedron. Cube: 6 + 8 − 12 = 2. Square pyramid: 5 + 5 − 8 = 2. The astonishing part is precisely that it does NOT depend on the solid.

questions.prompt: What is the TOP view of a cylinder standing upright?

options.text: An oval that is longer than it is wide
options.diagnosis: Perspective drawing habit; looking straight down, the rim is a true circle.
A view is a flat 2D picture, not the solid itself.

questions.explanation: Looking straight down at an upright cylinder you see only its circular top: the top view is a circle. The rectangle is its FRONT view. Each view flattens the solid from one direction.

questions.prompt: A polyhedron has 6 vertices and 12 edges. How many faces does it have?

options.diagnosis: Assumed faces must equal vertices; the relation, not symmetry, decides.
Sign slip while rearranging: computed E − V − 2 instead of 2 − V + E.

questions.explanation: F + V − E = 2 ⟹ F = 2 − V + E = 2 − 6 + 12 = 8. (This solid is the octahedron.) Rearranging as F = V + E − 2 gives 16 — a scrambled formula; check any rearrangement against the cube's 6 + 8 − 12 = 2.

nodes.title: Mensuration: Trapezium, Polygon Areas; Surface Area and Volume
nodes.description: You will find areas of trapeziums and general quadrilaterals via triangles, then step into 3D: surface areas and volumes of cuboids and cylinders. Keeping 'how much to paint' (surface area) separate from 'how much it holds' (volume) — and their different units — is the chapter's central discipline.
learning_outcomes: Can compute the area of a trapezium as ½(a + b)h and of polygons by triangulation
Can compute lateral/total surface area of cuboids, cubes and cylinders
Can compute volumes of cuboids, cubes and cylinders
Can choose between surface area and volume from context, with correct units (cm² vs cm³)
Can reason about scaling: doubling an edge multiplies volume by 8

misconceptions.description: Drops the ½ in the trapezium formula (or forgets to add the parallel sides first).
misconceptions.signal: Trapezium areas exactly double, or computed as product of the parallel sides.
misconceptions.remedy: Derive the formula by duplication: two copies of the trapezium (one rotated) form a parallelogram of base (a+b) and the same height — so the trapezium is HALF of (a+b)×h.

misconceptions.description: Confuses surface area with volume — computes one when the context needs the other.
misconceptions.signal: Uses volume to answer painting/wrapping questions; units of the answer don't match the quantity.
misconceptions.remedy: Sort a batch of real questions into PAINT (area, cm²) vs FILL (volume, cm³) before any formula work. Wrapping a box vs filling it with water makes the split physical.

misconceptions.description: Uses the curved-surface-area formula 2πrh when volume πr²h is needed (and vice versa) for cylinders.
misconceptions.signal: Cylinder answers linear in r for volume questions; the two formulas treated as interchangeable.
misconceptions.remedy: Dimension-check every formula before use: volume needs three lengths multiplied (r·r·h), surface area needs two (r·h or r·r). Unroll a paper label to SEE 2πr × h as a rectangle.

misconceptions.description: Assumes measures scale linearly: doubling a side doubles area and volume.
misconceptions.signal: Answers ×2 for the volume of a doubled cube; surprised a tank 'twice as big' holds 8 times the water.
misconceptions.remedy: Build the 2×2×2 block from 8 unit cubes — the eightfold jump is countable. Tabulate side, area, volume for sides 1, 2, 3 and read off the ×n² and ×n³ patterns.

real_world_hooks: Water tanker cylinders: how many litres fit? (1 L = 1000 cm³)
Painting a room vs the air inside it — area vs volume in one scene
Trapezium-shaped fields and canal cross-sections
Why a 'double-size' popcorn tub holds far more than double
teaching.video_search: trapezium area surface area volume cuboid cylinder class 8

questions.prompt: A trapezium has parallel sides 8 cm and 6 cm, and the distance between them is 5 cm. Its area is:

options.diagnosis: Multiplied all three numbers — no formula multiplies both parallel sides by the height.
Added all three measurements — a perimeter-style move, not an area one.

questions.explanation: Area = ½ × (sum of parallel sides) × height = ½ × (8 + 6) × 5 = ½ × 70 = 35 cm². Two copies of this trapezium tile a parallelogram of area 70 — hence the ½.

questions.prompt: Taking π = 22/7, find the VOLUME of a cylinder with radius 7 cm and height 10 cm.

options.diagnosis: Computed πrh — one r missing from the volume formula πr²h.
Computed the base area πr² but forgot to multiply by the height.

questions.explanation: V = πr²h = (22/7) × 7 × 7 × 10 = 22 × 7 × 10 = 1540 cm³. The value 440 is the CURVED SURFACE AREA 2πrh = 2 × (22/7) × 7 × 10 — the label, not the contents. Volume must multiply three lengths.

questions.prompt: The edge of a cube is DOUBLED. What happens to its volume?

options.diagnosis: Applied the AREA scaling factor (2²) to volume; volume scales with the cube, 2³.
Reached for the cube's 6 faces — a count of faces, not a scaling factor.

questions.explanation: Volume = edge³. New volume = (2e)³ = 8e³ — eight times the old. Concretely, a 2×2×2 stack contains exactly 8 unit cubes. (Surface area, by contrast, becomes 4 times as large: it scales with the square.)

nodes.title: Data Handling: Histograms, Pie Charts, Probability Intro
nodes.description: You will group data into class intervals and draw histograms (bars touching — the scale is continuous), build and read pie charts where slices are proportional shares of 360°, and compute probabilities of equally likely outcomes — learning why a coin has no memory.
learning_outcomes: Can group raw data into class intervals and draw/read a histogram
Can explain why histogram bars touch while bar-graph bars do not
Can convert data shares into pie-chart angles (fraction × 360°) and read pie charts
Can compute probabilities as favourable/total for equally likely outcomes, and recognise independence of successive trials

misconceptions.description: Treats a histogram as a bar graph: leaves gaps between bars, or reads class intervals as separate categories.
misconceptions.signal: Gapped 'histograms'; asks what the 'category' 20–30 means.
misconceptions.remedy: Contrast the two chart types on the same page: categories (fruit names) vs a continuous scale chopped into intervals (heights). The bars touch precisely because the intervals share endpoints on one number line.

misconceptions.description: Reads or draws pie-chart slices using the percentage AS the angle: a 25% share drawn as a 25° slice.
misconceptions.signal: Slice angles that total 100° instead of 360°.
misconceptions.remedy: Anchor the conversion: the whole circle is 360°, so a share s becomes s × 360°. Quick benchmarks help: 50% = 180°, 25% = 90°, 10% = 36°.

misconceptions.description: Gambler's fallacy: believes past random outcomes change future probabilities ('four heads in a row, so tails is due').
misconceptions.signal: Adjusts predicted probabilities after streaks; talks of luck 'evening out' on the next toss.
misconceptions.remedy: Simulate long runs of tosses (or use class data): after a streak of heads, the NEXT toss still lands heads about half the time. The coin has no memory — discuss why each toss is physically identical.

misconceptions.description: Forms probabilities as part-to-part odds instead of part-to-whole: P(red) = 3/7 from 3 red and 7 blue.
misconceptions.signal: Denominators equal to the OTHER group's count rather than the total.
misconceptions.remedy: Always write the sample space size first: 3 + 7 = 10 equally likely balls, THEN count favourables. Probability compares favourable outcomes with ALL outcomes.

real_world_hooks: Class heights or daily screen-time grouped into intervals — a real histogram
Monthly family budget as a pie chart: food, rent, travel, savings
Cricket toss streaks: does losing five tosses make you 'due' to win?
Board-game dice: chances of rolling the six you need
teaching.video_search: histogram pie chart central angle probability basics class 8

questions.prompt: A fair die is rolled once. What is the probability of getting a 3?

options.diagnosis: 'It happens or it doesn't' treated as two equally likely outcomes — but the six faces are the equally likely ones.
Used the face VALUE 3 as the count of favourable outcomes; only one face shows a 3.

questions.explanation: Six equally likely faces, one favourable: P(3) = 1/6. The denominator counts ALL outcomes (6), not the unfavourable ones (5) — and the number printed on the face has nothing to do with how many faces are favourable.

questions.prompt: In a pie chart of a family budget, food takes 25% of total spending. What central angle should the food slice have?

options.diagnosis: Halved the correct angle — possibly used 180° as the whole circle.
Computed 100 − 25 and then read the result as degrees — two confusions chained.

questions.explanation: The full circle is 360°, so 25% of it is 0.25 × 360 = 90°. Percentages and degrees are different scales for shares: 25 out of 100 corresponds to 90 out of 360.

questions.prompt: A fair coin has landed heads 4 times in a row. What is the probability that the NEXT toss is a head?

options.text: Less than 1/2, because tails is now 'due'
More than 1/2, because heads is on a hot streak

options.diagnosis: That is the probability of five heads in a row computed BEFORE any tosses — not the probability of the next single toss given four already happened.

questions.explanation: The coin has no memory: the next toss is the same physical experiment as always, so P(head) = 1/2. The streak's rarity (1/32 for five in advance) is irrelevant once four heads have already occurred — both 'due for tails' and 'hot streak' are versions of the gambler's fallacy.
